questions.prompt: What does the author recommend?
questions.passage:
Ask students how they prepare for an exam and most will describe some form of rereading: going over their notes, reading the chapter one more time, highlighting as they go. Ask psychologists what works and you will hear something rather different. One of the most robust findings in the study of memory is that trying to recall material—answering questions on it, or writing down what one remembers without looking—fixes it in the mind for longer than reading it again does. Rereading remains popular because it feels productive: the text grows more familiar each time, and familiarity is easily mistaken for knowledge. Recall, by contrast, feels like failure, because it exposes how much one has forgotten.

Replacing final exams with a larger number of smaller graded tests
Teaching students to reread their notes in a more active and critical way
No longer using tests to find out what students have actually learned

questions.prompt: What is the main point of the text?
questions.passage:
Every spring, volunteers in parks and nature reserves across much of Europe spend their weekends pulling up plants that are judged not to belong. The work is often described in military language. Unwanted species are 'invaders' or 'aliens'; they 'colonise' riverbanks and 'conquer' woodland; the volunteers who uproot them are fighting a 'war'. The vocabulary is so familiar that it is easy to forget it is a choice, and one that carries an argument within it: that a species which arrived with human help is, for that reason alone, an enemy.

Some introduced species have certainly earned the hostility. When the brown tree snake reached the Pacific island of Guam, probably as a stowaway in military cargo shortly after the Second World War, it found an abundance of birds that had never had to deal with a climbing predator. Within a few decades most of the island's native forest birds had disappeared. Stories like this are the reason why biologists take introductions seriously, and they are not rare.

They are, however, unrepresentative. Of all the species that people carry to new places, deliberately or by accident, the great majority fail to survive in the wild at all. Of those that do survive, most remain local and unremarkable, and only a small fraction go on to spread widely and cause serious harm. Ecologists have long used a rough rule of thumb according to which only about one species in ten passes each of these stages. The figures vary greatly from one group of organisms to another, but the general pattern holds: being non-native is common, and being harmful is not. A label that applies equally to the brown tree snake and to a garden flower that has quietly grown in a few hedgerows for two centuries tells us very little about either.

The label is also less precise than it sounds. To call a species native is to say that it was present before some point in time, but which point? In Britain, botanists treat plants that arrived before about 1500 more or less as natives, and several well-loved cornfield flowers would fail a stricter test. As the climate warms, the question becomes harder still. Species are now shifting their ranges northwards without anyone's help, and it is not obvious whether a butterfly that crosses the Channel under its own power should be welcomed as a refugee or resisted as an intruder. Meanwhile, some undoubtedly native species do great damage when circumstances change: deer, freed from the predators that people removed long ago, can strip a woodland of its young trees as thoroughly as any newcomer.

None of this means that origin is irrelevant. A species that evolved elsewhere has not been tested against the predators, parasites and competitors it will meet in its new home, and the consequences of its arrival are therefore harder to predict. Moreover, prevention is far cheaper than cure. Once a species has become established over a wide area, removing it may be impossible at any price, while checking cargo and banning the sale of risky plants costs relatively little. At the border, then, treating unfamiliar species with suspicion is simply prudent.

The mistake is to carry the same reasoning into places where it no longer applies. A plant that has lived in a region for a hundred years is no longer an unknown quantity; its effects can be observed rather than guessed at. If it crowds out other species, damages riverbanks or poisons livestock, there is a case for controlling it. If it does none of these things, the fact that it came from somewhere else is not, by itself, a reason to spend scarce money and volunteer time on removing it, money and time that might be used against a native species that is doing real harm.

What the military vocabulary obscures is that conservation is ultimately about choices: which landscapes we want, which losses we are prepared to accept, and where limited resources will do the most good. Asking where a species came from is a useful first question. Treating it as the last one turns a matter of judgement into a matter of identity, and that is rarely a good basis for any decision.
options: Military language has made the public more hostile to introduced species than most biologists are.
Introduced species are rarely harmful, so money spent on controlling them would do more good elsewhere.
A species' origin is a better guide to keeping new species out than to dealing with established ones.
The idea of a native species has lost its meaning now that a warming climate is moving species around.
questions.explain: The author accepts that suspicion of unfamiliar species is 'simply prudent' at the border, since newcomers are unpredictable and prevention is cheap, but argues that a species which has lived in a region for a long time should be judged by its observed effects, not by where it came from: origin is 'a useful first question' but should not be the last. The text does say that most introduced species are harmless, but the conclusion that money spent on controlling them would be better used elsewhere goes too far: the author supports checking cargo and banning risky plants, and says there is a case for controlling an established plant that does harm. Nothing suggests that biologists are less hostile than the public; the text says they 'take introductions seriously'. And although a warming climate makes the question of what is native 'harder still', the author does not conclude that the idea has lost its meaning, but goes on to defend origin as relevant at the border.

questions.prompt: What does the reviewer appreciate about Coyle's portrayal of Robert FitzRoy?
questions.passage:
Weather forecasts are among the few scientific predictions that most of us consult every day, and among the few we feel entitled to mock. Harriet Coyle's Tomorrow's Sky, a history of the forecast from the first newspaper predictions to the present, sets out to explain how something so routine came to be possible, and why it still so often feels unreliable.

The book is at its best in its first half, which follows a handful of people who tried to predict the weather before anyone was sure it could be done. Coyle is particularly good on Robert FitzRoy, the naval officer who began publishing daily forecasts in The Times in 1861 and was mocked in the press whenever they failed. She resists the temptation to make him a martyr to science. Her FitzRoy is stubborn and thin-skinned, as quick to blame his critics as his instruments, and all the more sympathetic for it. Equally memorable is her account of Lewis Fry Richardson, who during the First World War spent weeks working out by hand a forecast for a single six-hour period, using the kind of physical equations that computers now solve. His result was wildly wrong, and Coyle shows with real skill why the failure was more instructive than many successes: his method was sound, but the data and the arithmetic available to him were not up to it.

The trouble begins when the story reaches the age in which the method finally worked. The arrival of satellites and electronic computers, which turned a speculative craft into a reliable service, is covered in a single chapter, and a hurried one. A reader would learn more from a few pages of a decent textbook about how today's forecasts are actually made. It is hard not to suspect that Coyle simply finds the earlier period more congenial: it has more eccentrics in it, and fewer committees.

That preference also shapes the argument that runs through the book. Coyle's central claim is that the history of forecasting is a history of learning to be uncertain. Early forecasters offered confident statements and were ridiculed when these turned out wrong; their modern successors speak of a seventy per cent chance of rain, and in doing so tell us something more honest about what can be known. It is an attractive idea, and in places a genuinely illuminating one. But it is repeated so often, and applied to so many episodes, that it begins to look less like a conclusion than a lens fitted before the evidence was examined. Forecasters did not, after all, begin to express themselves in probabilities simply because they became more modest. They did so in large part because they acquired the means of calculating those probabilities, and those means are exactly what the hurried chapter leaves out.

Coyle writes clear and often elegant prose, though she is too fond of meteorological metaphor; by the time a disagreement between two committees had been described as 'a cold front moving through the department', this reader was longing for plainer language. Such lapses are minor. The larger problem is one of balance, and it is a pity, because the material she has chosen to dwell on is handled with real distinction.

Tomorrow's Sky is, in the end, a fine book about the past of forecasting and a thin one about its present. Readers who want to know why the forecast on their phone is so much better than it was a generation ago will have to look elsewhere. Those who want to know why anyone attempted it in the first place could hardly do better.
options: It shows how unfairly the press treated a pioneer of science.
It presents him as a flawed man rather than as a heroic victim.
It explains why his forecasts were better than his critics thought.
It shows that his stubbornness was the key to his later success.
questions.explain: The reviewer praises Coyle for resisting 'the temptation to make him a martyr to science': her FitzRoy is 'stubborn and thin-skinned' and 'all the more sympathetic for it', so he appears as a man with faults rather than as a heroic victim. Saying that the book shows how unfairly the press treated him reverses this point, since portraying him as wronged by his critics is exactly the martyr's story Coyle avoids. The review does not say that his forecasts were better than his critics believed, and his stubbornness is presented as a flaw of character, not as the reason for any success.

questions.prompt: What is the main point of the text?
questions.passage:
Anyone who has spent a night on a hospital ward will remember the noise. Monitors beep when a patient's heart rate rises or falls, infusion pumps chime when a bag runs empty, and sensors sound when a clip slips off a finger. Each of these alarms exists for a good reason, and each was added by someone who wanted to make patients safer. Taken together, however, they may be doing the opposite.

The problem is not that alarms fail to go off, but that they go off far too often. Studies of intensive care units have repeatedly found that most alarms require no action at all: the patient has moved, a cable has come loose, or a reading has briefly crossed a limit and returned to normal of its own accord. Staff who hear hundreds of such signals in a shift learn, quite reasonably, that an alarm usually means nothing. They respond more slowly, silence devices without checking, or widen the limits until the machines fall quiet. Nurses call this alarm fatigue, and it has been linked to cases in which a genuine emergency went unnoticed because the signal announcing it sounded exactly like the hundred false ones that preceded it.

A manufacturer who sets a monitor to sound at the slightest irregularity is protected if something goes wrong; a manufacturer who sets it to stay quiet is not. questions.prompt: According to the text, what weakness do some scholars see in the painted reconstructions?
questions.passage:
The white marble statues of ancient Greece and Rome have long stood for a particular ideal of beauty: calm, pure and free of decoration. Yet many of them were never meant to be white. Traces of pigment survive on a great number of ancient sculptures, and with the help of ultraviolet light and chemical analysis researchers have been able to reconstruct patterned clothing, coloured eyes and painted skin. The ancients, it seems, painted their statues, and often brightly.

Reconstructions based on this evidence regularly provoke dismay. Visitors to exhibitions of painted copies have described them as garish, even vulgar, and some scholars have objected that the reconstructions rest on so little surviving paint that they are partly guesswork. That objection has some force: a fleck of blue on a fold of drapery does not reveal the exact shade, or how it was combined with other colours. But the discomfort seems to have older roots. The admiration for white marble took shape in the eighteenth century, when the paint had long since weathered away, and writers who knew the statues only in their faded state built a whole theory of classical taste largely on that absence. What looks like a reaction to bad reconstruction may often be loyalty to that theory.
options: Much of what they show cannot be read from the surviving traces of paint.
They use pigments that would not have been available in antiquity.
They may reproduce paint that was added long after the statues were made.
Their colours are brighter than modern visitors find tasteful.
questions.explain: Some scholars object that the reconstructions 'rest on so little surviving paint that they are partly guesswork', and the author agrees that a fleck of blue does not reveal the exact shade or how it was combined with other colours; much of what the copies show must therefore be filled in. The text says nothing about anachronistic pigments or about paint added after antiquity. The complaint that the colours are garish comes from visitors, not from the scholars, and concerns taste rather than evidence.

questions.prompt: Which alternative best fits gap 1?
questions.passage:
For most of history, repairing things was not a hobby or a political statement but simply what people did. Shoes were resoled, clothes were patched, and radios went back to the shop when they stopped working. Today the same instinct often meets an obstacle that has little to do with skill. Many products are designed in ways that make repair __1__: batteries are glued in place, parts are fixed with unusual screws, and spare components are sold only to authorised workshops, if at all.

Manufacturers argue that these choices are not meant to discourage repair. Gluing a battery makes a phone thinner, sealing a case keeps out water, and restricting access to parts protects customers from poor workmanship. Some of these arguments are __2__. A sealed phone does survive a fall into a puddle better than one held together with clips. But they explain less than they claim to. A thinner phone does not require that a replacement screen be paired electronically with the original circuit board, so that a perfectly good part fitted by an independent repairer refuses to work.

The movement for a 'right to repair' therefore asks for something quite __3__. It does not demand that products be built to last forever, or that good design give way to durability. It asks that owners and independent workshops have access to the same parts, tools and manuals as the manufacturer's own technicians. __4__, it asks that a product, once bought, should belong to the person who bought it.
questions.explain: The preceding sentence speaks of an 'obstacle' that has 'little to do with skill', and the examples after the colon (glued batteries, unusual screws, spare parts that are hard to get) all make repairing a product difficult, so the design makes repair 'impractical'. 'Unnecessary' would mean that products no longer need repairing, but the examples hinder repair rather than remove the need for it. 'Hazardous' does not fit, since the examples are presented as obstacles rather than dangers: unusual screws and restricted spare parts make repair harder, not riskier, and the risk to customers mentioned later is poor workmanship. 'Unpopular' would concern people's attitudes, whereas the paragraph is about obstacles built into the products themselves.

questions.prompt: Why, according to the text, had it been difficult to explain the home advantage before 2020?
questions.passage:
For as long as statistics have been kept, teams in most sports have won more often at home than away. Explanations have never been in short supply. Players sleep in their own beds and avoid tiring journeys; they know the quirks of their own pitch; and, above all, they are cheered on by thousands of supporters. Until recently there was no way of separating these factors, because they almost always came together. Then, in 2020, the pandemic forced football leagues across Europe to play their matches in empty stadiums, and researchers suddenly had an experiment they could never have arranged themselves.

The results were striking. In several leagues the home advantage shrank noticeably, and in some it seemed to disappear altogether. More revealing than the size of the change, however, was where it showed up. The way the teams themselves played changed less clearly than one might have expected. What changed most consistently was the behaviour of referees, who in many leagues now showed visiting players fewer yellow cards, relative to home players, than before. The roar of the crowd, it seems, had been working less on the players it was meant to encourage than on the official it was meant to intimidate.

It would be a mistake, though, to treat the matter as settled. The season was hardly normal in other respects: matches were crammed into a short period, travel was restricted, and players were living under unusual rules. Nor did every league show the same pattern, and in a few the home advantage barely changed. And the advantage had in any case been shrinking slowly for decades, perhaps because easier travel and more uniform pitches had eroded some of its older causes. The empty stadiums showed that crowds matter. They could not show how much, or that they matter in the same way everywhere.
options: Statistics on away matches had not been collected systematically.
Researchers disagreed about how the advantage should be measured.
The possible causes were hardly ever found apart from one another.
The advantage differed too much between sports to have a single cause.
questions.explain: The text lists several possible explanations (rest, familiarity with the pitch, supporters) and says there was 'no way of separating these factors, because they almost always came together'. In other words, the possible causes were hardly ever found apart, so their effects could not be told apart either. The empty stadiums of 2020 changed that by removing one of them, the crowds. The text states that statistics have long been kept and says nothing about how they were collected for away matches. No disagreement about measurement is mentioned, and the advantage is described as common to 'most sports', not as differing between them.

questions.prompt: What does the author mean by saying that crowd figures are 'easy to bend without anyone telling an outright lie'?
questions.passage:
After almost every large demonstration, two numbers appear. The organisers announce one, the police another, and the gap between them is often so wide that it is tempting to assume both are invented. In fact, counting a crowd is not especially mysterious. The standard method, developed in the 1960s, is to divide the area the crowd occupies into sections, estimate how densely people are packed in a sample of them, and multiply. A loosely gathered crowd might have one person per square metre; in a tightly packed one, where people can barely move, there may be four or more.

The arithmetic is simple. The difficulty lies in the inputs, and especially in density, which varies enormously across a single crowd. The area just in front of a stage may be packed solid while the edges are thin, and an estimate that takes the dense centre as typical can easily double the true figure. Marches create a further problem, because people come and go. A count of everyone present at the moment of peak attendance will miss those who joined for an hour and left early, while adding up everyone who passes a given point risks counting the same people twice if the route loops back on itself.

None of this means that the figures are arbitrary, but it does mean that they are easy to bend without anyone telling an outright lie. Organisers have an obvious interest in large numbers and authorities sometimes in small ones, and each side can choose, honestly enough, the assumptions that suit it. Independent estimates based on aerial photographs tend to fall between the two, though not always in the middle.

The most useful question to ask about a crowd figure, then, is not whether it is true, but how it was produced. A number that comes with its method attached (the area measured, the densities assumed, the time of day) can be checked and argued with. A number without one can only be believed or disbelieved, and people tend to believe whichever figure flatters the cause they already support.
options: Organisers and the police often agree in private on figures other than those they publish.
Different but defensible assumptions can produce very different totals.
Small errors in counting tend to grow as figures are passed on to the press.
The figures are often rounded up in ways that are difficult to detect.
questions.explain: The next sentence explains the remark: each side 'can choose, honestly enough, the assumptions that suit it'. Because density and attendance vary so much, reasonable choices of input can lead to very different totals without anyone inventing a number. Private agreements between organisers and the police are never mentioned. The text does not describe errors growing as figures are passed on, and rounding up is not discussed; the point concerns the assumptions behind the calculation.

questions.prompt: Why, according to the text, did Ise once seem 'a puzzle, even a scandal' to many European conservationists?
questions.passage:
At Ise, the most sacred buildings of Japan's most important Shinto shrine are taken down roughly every twenty years and rebuilt, in fresh cypress wood, on a neighbouring plot. The practice has continued, with some interruptions, for well over a thousand years. The buildings a visitor sees today are therefore no more than about twenty years old, and yet they are widely regarded as one of the oldest living traditions of Japanese architecture.

To many European conservationists, this once seemed a puzzle, even a scandal. Their own tradition held that what deserves protection is original material: the stones actually laid by medieval masons, the timbers actually cut in the year a church was built. Replacing such material, however faithfully, was thought to destroy precisely what made a building valuable. By that standard, Ise has nothing left to protect.

Yet the rebuilding preserves something that the European approach can lose. Each reconstruction requires carpenters who know the old techniques, and the twenty-year cycle ensures that the knowledge is passed on before those who hold it grow too old to work. A medieval church whose every original beam has been carefully preserved may stand intact while the skills needed to build it have long since vanished. Since the 1990s, international guidelines on heritage have recognised that authenticity can reside in form, use and tradition as well as in material. Ise did not change its practice to fit that view; the view, in part, was changed to make room for Ise.
options: The rebuilding destroyed buildings that had stood for over a thousand years.
The new buildings were not faithful copies of the ones they replaced.
They doubted that the tradition had really continued without interruption.
They located a building's value in the material it was originally made of.
questions.explain: The European tradition held that 'what deserves protection is original material', and that replacing it 'however faithfully' destroys what makes a building valuable; buildings that are replaced every twenty years thus seemed to have 'nothing left to protect'. It is the practice of rebuilding, not the buildings, that is over a thousand years old; each building stands for only about twenty years. The text does not suggest that the new buildings are unfaithful copies, and the phrase 'however faithfully' shows that even faithful copies would not have satisfied the European view. The interruptions are mentioned by the author and are not presented as the source of the conservationists' objection.

questions.prompt: What is the main point of the text?
questions.passage:
Economists who want to show that markets can lock in an inferior technology have for decades reached for the same example: the keyboard on which this text was typed. The QWERTY layout, the story goes, was designed in the 1870s for mechanical typewriters whose type bars jammed when neighbouring keys were struck in quick succession, and it deliberately separated common pairs of letters in order to slow typists down. The jamming problem disappeared long ago, and in the 1930s an American educational psychologist, August Dvorak, patented a layout that placed the most frequently used letters on the middle row, directly under the typist's fingers. Tests showed that typists trained on it worked dramatically faster. Yet QWERTY survived, because everyone had learned it, every machine used it, and no one could afford to be the first to switch.

It is an elegant story, and its lesson, that an early accident can become permanent even when something better is available, has been applied to everything from video formats to railway gauges. In an influential paper in the 1980s, the economist Paul David used it to argue that history matters to economics in a way that standard models had overlooked: the path a market takes can determine where it ends up.

The difficulty is that almost every part of the story has been questioned. The claim that QWERTY was designed to slow typists down rests on thin evidence; the arrangement seems to have emerged from a long series of practical adjustments, among them attempts to reduce jamming, and fewer jams may well have made typists faster rather than slower. More seriously, the tests that showed Dvorak's layout to be far superior were, for the most part, carried out or supervised by Dvorak himself, who had a patent to sell. A later study run by the United States government in the 1950s found that retraining experienced typists on the new layout brought gains too small to justify the cost, and later comparisons have generally found the differences to be modest.

If that is right, the keyboard is not an example of a market trapped with an inferior product, but of a market that declined to pay for an improvement too small to be worth the trouble. That would be a rather different lesson, and a less dramatic one.

Defenders of the original argument have a reasonable reply. Path dependence, they point out, never required the losing technology to be dramatically better; it only requires that early choices constrain later ones, which in the case of the keyboard they plainly do. Nobody who learned to type on QWERTY is eager to start again. That is true, but it rather changes the subject. What made the keyboard such a powerful illustration was not the modest claim that habits are costly to change, which few would dispute, but the stronger claim that whole markets can be stuck with a clearly worse choice. For that claim the keyboard, it now seems, is a weak witness.

None of this shows that markets never lock in inferior technologies. It shows something narrower and perhaps more useful: that a story can become famous because it illustrates an idea well, and then be cited as evidence for the idea it was chosen to illustrate. The more perfectly an example fits a theory, the more carefully it may deserve to be checked.
options: The idea that markets can lock in inferior technologies has been shown to be mistaken.
The keyboard gives far weaker support to the idea of lock-in than its fame suggests.
QWERTY survived because it was in fact better suited to typing than its rivals.
Economists have exaggerated how costly it is for typists to learn a new layout.
questions.explain: The author shows that most parts of the famous keyboard story have been questioned and concludes that, for the claim that markets can be stuck with a clearly worse choice, the keyboard 'is a weak witness'. The author explicitly says that 'none of this shows that markets never lock in inferior technologies', so the idea itself is not rejected. The text does not claim that QWERTY is better; the critics' view is that the alternative offered only a small improvement. And the cost of relearning is not said to be exaggerated: the government study found the gains too small to justify that cost, and the author accepts that habits are 'costly to change'.

questions.prompt: What is the main point of the text?
questions.passage:
Few environmental pledges photograph as well as a promise to plant trees. A politician with a spade, a row of saplings, a number with plenty of zeros: the image suggests a problem being solved by hand, one seedling at a time. Trees do draw carbon dioxide out of the air and store it in wood and soil, and forests do much else besides, from holding hillsides together to sheltering wildlife. It is easy to see why planting has become a favourite climate gesture of governments and companies alike.

The difficulty lies less in the trees than in the counting. A pledge is usually measured in saplings put into the ground, because that is the figure that can be announced on the day. But a sapling is not a forest. In dry years, or where nobody is paid to water and weed, a large share of young trees may die within a few seasons, and a campaign that reports what was planted rather than what survived can claim success for a hillside that is bare again a decade later. Even the trees that live take decades to store the carbon with which they are credited at the outset, while the emissions they are meant to make up for enter the atmosphere at once.

Where the trees go matters as much as how many there are. Planting on land that was forest until recently can restore much of what was lost. Planting on natural grassland or peat bog is another matter. Such landscapes may look empty to a visitor, but many hold large amounts of carbon below ground and support species found nowhere else; covering them with fast-growing conifers can release some of that carbon and drive out the very wildlife a project claims to help. In snowy regions, a dark canopy that replaces pale ground can even absorb more of the sun's heat, cancelling part of the cooling the trees provide.

None of this means that planting is pointless. It means that the number on the press release is a poor guide to the benefit. Several researchers have argued that the cheapest and most reliable way to gain a forest is often not to plant one at all but to let one return: to protect land from grazing or clearing and allow trees to seed themselves, as they will in many places if left alone. Such forests are less dramatic to launch and harder to photograph, since for the first few years there is little to show but scrub. They also tend to suit local conditions better, because the trees that arrive are the ones the land can support.

The deepest worry, however, concerns not the trees but what they may excuse. A company that promises to plant its way to 'net zero' is making a claim about the future in exchange for permission to go on emitting in the present. Forests can burn, be felled or die in a drought, and the carbon in them can return to the air far more quickly than it was stored. Planting is best seen as an addition to cutting emissions rather than a substitute for it—a useful thing to do with a spade, provided the spade is not also used to bury the question of what comes out of the chimney.
options: Tree planting has become popular mainly because it is so easy to present well to the public.
Letting forests return by themselves works better than planting trees in almost every case.
Tree-planting pledges tend to promise more for the climate than they can reliably deliver.
Planting trees does the climate more harm than good when it is done on the wrong kind of land.
questions.explain: The author accepts that trees store carbon and that planting is not 'pointless', but argues that the figures announced say little about the real benefit: many saplings die, carbon is stored only slowly, planting in the wrong place can backfire, and promises to plant may excuse continued emissions. Pledges therefore tend to promise more than planting can reliably deliver. That planting is popular because it photographs well is said in the first paragraph, but only as the starting point for the argument. Letting forests return is said to be 'often' the cheapest and most reliable option, not better in almost every case. Planting on grassland or bog is one problem among several, and the author does not claim that it does more harm than good overall.

questions.prompt: Why does the author begin with the example of the twenty research teams?
questions.passage:
Imagine twenty research teams, working independently, all testing whether a certain food supplement improves memory. Suppose it does nothing at all. By the ordinary rules of statistics, which accept a one-in-twenty risk of mistaking chance for a real effect, one of the teams can be expected, on average, to find a 'significant' result anyway. That team writes up its study, and a journal, pleased with a clear and surprising finding, publishes it. The other nineteen, with nothing to report but a flat line, put their data in a drawer and move on. Anyone who later searches the literature will find a single study, and it will say that the supplement works.

This is the 'file-drawer problem', and it does not require anyone to cheat. Each decision along the way is understandable. Researchers have limited time and would rather spend it on work that might be published; editors want papers that others will cite; and a study reporting that something has no effect can seem, to all concerned, like a study in which nothing happened. Yet the sum of these sensible choices is a record that systematically overstates how often things work, and the distortion is invisible from inside, because the missing studies leave no trace.

Several remedies have been tried. Some journals now accept papers on the basis of the question and the methods, before any results exist, and promise to publish whatever the data turn out to show. In some fields, trials must be registered before they begin, so that a study which quietly disappears can at least be seen to be missing. Statisticians have devised ways of estimating, from the pattern of published results, how many unpublished ones there are likely to be, though such estimates rest on assumptions that are hard to check.

What these measures have in common is that they change not the honesty of researchers but the incentives around them. That is probably the right target. Appeals to publish negative results have been made for decades, with little effect, because they ask individuals to bear a cost for a benefit that is shared by everyone. A null result that is published is a small gift to the field: it saves others from repeating a dead end and corrects the impression left by luckier studies. The trouble is that, under the present system, the researcher who gives that gift is rarely the one who is thanked for it.
options: To show how easily researchers are tempted to report their data dishonestly.
To suggest that studies of food supplements are especially unreliable.
To argue that most of the findings published in science are probably false.
To show how a false impression can arise even if every study is honest.
questions.explain: In the example no one does anything wrong: one team finds a 'significant' result by chance, the others leave their results unpublished, and the literature ends up saying that a useless supplement works. The author then stresses that the problem 'does not require anyone to cheat'. The example thus shows how a misleading picture can arise from honest studies, which rules out the reading that it is about dishonest reporting. The supplement is merely an illustration, and nothing suggests that such studies are especially unreliable. The text says that the record overstates how often things work, which is not the same as claiming that most published findings are false.

questions.prompt: According to the text, what does registering trials before they begin achieve?
questions.passage:
Imagine twenty research teams, working independently, all testing whether a certain food supplement improves memory. Suppose it does nothing at all. By the ordinary rules of statistics, which accept a one-in-twenty risk of mistaking chance for a real effect, one of the teams can be expected, on average, to find a 'significant' result anyway. That team writes up its study, and a journal, pleased with a clear and surprising finding, publishes it. The other nineteen, with nothing to report but a flat line, put their data in a drawer and move on. Anyone who later searches the literature will find a single study, and it will say that the supplement works.

This is the 'file-drawer problem', and it does not require anyone to cheat. Each decision along the way is understandable. Researchers have limited time and would rather spend it on work that might be published; editors want papers that others will cite; and a study reporting that something has no effect can seem, to all concerned, like a study in which nothing happened. Yet the sum of these sensible choices is a record that systematically overstates how often things work, and the distortion is invisible from inside, because the missing studies leave no trace.

Several remedies have been tried. Some journals now accept papers on the basis of the question and the methods, before any results exist, and promise to publish whatever the data turn out to show. In some fields, trials must be registered before they begin, so that a study which quietly disappears can at least be seen to be missing. Statisticians have devised ways of estimating, from the pattern of published results, how many unpublished ones there are likely to be, though such estimates rest on assumptions that are hard to check.

What these measures have in common is that they change not the honesty of researchers but the incentives around them. That is probably the right target. Appeals to publish negative results have been made for decades, with little effect, because they ask individuals to bear a cost for a benefit that is shared by everyone. A null result that is published is a small gift to the field: it saves others from repeating a dead end and corrects the impression left by luckier studies. The trouble is that, under the present system, the researcher who gives that gift is rarely the one who is thanked for it.
options: It ensures that every study is published whatever its results turn out to be.
It allows statisticians to work out how many studies have gone unpublished.
It makes it possible to notice when a study has never been reported.
It persuades researchers to publish results that show no effect at all.
questions.explain: Registration means that 'a study which quietly disappears can at least be seen to be missing', so it becomes possible to notice when a study has never been reported. A promise to publish whatever the results show is made by the journals that accept papers before results exist, which is a different remedy. Estimating the number of unpublished studies from the pattern of published ones is the statisticians' method, which the text does not link to registration. The words 'at least' show that registration does not make the missing study appear, so it is not presented as getting researchers to publish their null results.

questions.passage:
When engines, lamps or furnaces become more efficient, it seems obvious that we will use less energy. Yet economists have long pointed out that the savings are often smaller than the engineers' figures promise. __1__ a more efficient car is cheaper to run per kilometre, its owner may choose to drive further, or to buy a larger model, and some of the fuel saved is used up again. This is known as the rebound effect, and its size has been a matter of __2__ among researchers, with estimates ranging from a small fraction of the expected saving to more than all of it. For most household appliances, studies suggest that the rebound swallows only part of the saving: a more efficient fridge is not, after all, an invitation to keep more food cold. In other cases the picture is less reassuring. When a technology becomes so cheap to use that entirely new uses for it appear, total consumption can even rise—the outcome now known as the Jevons paradox, after the nineteenth-century economist William Stanley Jevons, who __3__ it for coal as steam engines grew more economical.

None of this is an argument against efficiency. It is an argument against treating it as a solution in __4__. Unless greater efficiency is combined with measures that stop energy, or the pollution it causes, from becoming cheaper to use, part of its benefit is likely to leak away.

'Unless' would make the extra driving depend on the car not being cheaper to run, which makes no sense.

questions.prompt: What is the main point of the text?
questions.passage: Laboratory mice are usually kept in rooms set to a temperature that feels comfortable to the people who work there. For a mouse, however, such a room is chilly: a small animal loses heat quickly, and a mouse in a typical animal house must burn a good deal of extra energy simply to stay warm. Some researchers have begun to ask what this does to their results. An animal that is constantly working to keep itself warm differs from a comfortable one in its metabolism, and possibly in the way its immune system behaves and how it responds to some drugs. If so, some findings may owe something to the thermostat as well as to the treatment being tested. Raising the temperature is not a simple fix—the people who look after the animals would then have to work in uncomfortable heat—but the question has at least made clear that 'standard conditions' are standard mainly for the humans.
options: Laboratory mice suffer needlessly because the rooms they live in are kept too cold.
Results from studies on mice cannot be relied on to apply to human beings.
A routine detail of laboratory life may have been quietly affecting results.
Animal houses should be heated to a temperature that suits mice rather than staff.
questions.explain: The text describes how the ordinary room temperature in animal houses, chosen to suit the staff, forces mice to spend energy keeping warm, which may change their metabolism and their responses, so that 'some findings may owe something to the thermostat'. A routine detail may thus have been influencing results without anyone noticing. The text is concerned with what the cold does to research results, not with the animals' suffering. Nor does it say that results from mice cannot be applied to humans; the comparison is between cold and comfortable mice, and 'the humans' at the end refers to the staff. Finally, the author says that raising the temperature 'is not a simple fix', so the text does not recommend it.

questions.prompt: According to the text, why might removing a few large dead objects do more good than catching many small fragments?
questions.passage: Low orbit around the earth is often imagined as empty, but it is becoming crowded. Alongside working satellites circle dead ones, spent rocket stages and countless fragments too small to track yet large enough, at orbital speeds, to wreck a spacecraft. Each collision between two large objects produces thousands of new fragments, each capable of causing further collisions. Some scientists fear that at the busiest altitudes the process could eventually sustain itself, so that debris would go on multiplying even if no further launches took place. Removing a few of the largest dead objects would do more to prevent this than catching a great many small fragments, since it is the large objects that would feed the chain. Yet removing even one such object is difficult and costly, and it is far from clear who should pay.
options: Collisions involving large objects would supply most of the new debris.
Small fragments are far too numerous for any clean-up to make a difference.
Large objects are easier to track and therefore cheaper to bring down.
Small fragments cause little damage compared with the large dead objects.
questions.explain: The text says that removing a few large objects would help more 'since it is the large objects that would feed the chain': each collision between two large objects produces thousands of new fragments. It never says that small fragments are too numerous to deal with; it only argues that removing large objects would do more. That small fragments are hard to track is mentioned, but nothing suggests that large objects are cheap to remove, and removal is called 'difficult and costly'. Small fragments are described as able to wreck a spacecraft, so they cannot be said to cause little damage.

questions.prompt: What does the author mean by saying that the label 'describes what the material can do, not what will happen to it'?
questions.passage: A coffee cup labelled 'compostable' sounds like the end of a problem. Often it is the start of another. Many such materials break down only under the conditions of an industrial composting plant, where heat and moisture are carefully controlled; in a garden heap, a hedge or the sea they may persist for years. If they are collected with ordinary plastic, they can contaminate batches meant for recycling; if they are sent to a composting plant that is not equipped for them, they may be screened out and burned. The label, in other words, describes what the material can do, not what will happen to it. Whether a 'compostable' cup is better than an ordinary one depends less on its chemistry than on what lies at the other end of the bin.
options: Makers often claim properties for their materials that have never been tested.
Compostable materials break down more slowly than their labels would suggest.
Most people throw compostable cups into the wrong kind of bin by mistake.
Whether the cup really breaks down depends on how it is handled after use.
questions.explain: The author explains that many such materials break down only in an industrial composting plant and may persist for years elsewhere, or be screened out and burned. The label thus states a property of the material, but whether the cup is ever composted depends on where it ends up. Nothing suggests that the claims on such labels are untested or false: under the right conditions the material does break down. Persisting 'for years' happens in a garden heap, a hedge or the sea, not under the conditions that the label refers to. And the text describes what can happen to cups in different bins without saying what most people actually do with them.

questions.prompt: What is the purpose of the 'refuges' described in the text?
questions.passage: When a crop is engineered to produce its own insecticide, the pests that feed on it come under strong pressure to evolve resistance. One defence seems at first to work against the farmer: alongside the protected crop, strips of an ordinary variety are planted on which insects can feed freely. These 'refuges' sacrifice part of the harvest. Their purpose is to keep susceptible insects plentiful, so that the rare resistant individuals that survive on the protected crop are likely to mate with susceptible ones rather than with each other. Where resistance depends on a gene that must be inherited from both parents, the offspring of such pairs remain vulnerable to the insecticide. The strategy rests on assumptions about the pests' genetics and habits that do not hold everywhere, and in some regions resistance has spread regardless.
options: To give farmers a harvest to fall back on if pests destroy the protected crop.
To reduce the chance that resistant insects will produce resistant offspring.
To lure the pests away from the protected crop so that it suffers less damage.
To make it possible to spot resistant insects before they spread through a region.
questions.explain: The refuges keep susceptible insects plentiful so that resistant survivors are likely to mate with them, and where resistance must be inherited from both parents, the offspring of such pairs 'remain vulnerable'. The purpose is thus to make resistant offspring less likely. The refuges are said to 'sacrifice part of the harvest', not to keep a reserve harvest. Nor are they meant to draw pests away from the protected crop; what matters is which insects mate with each other, not where they feed. Nothing is said about using refuges to detect resistant insects.

questions.prompt: What point is made in the final sentence of the text?
questions.passage: In the last days of 1999, programmers around the world were still at work on a problem that had been building for decades. To save what was once costly memory, many older systems stored years as two digits, so that the year after 1999 risked being read as 1900, with unpredictable consequences for anything that calculated with dates. Governments and companies spent large sums checking and repairing their software. When the new year arrived and little of note went wrong, many people concluded that the danger had been exaggerated, and the episode is still sometimes cited as an example of needless alarm. Those who did the work tend to draw the opposite conclusion. The trouble with a successful prevention, they point out, is that its success looks exactly like the absence of a problem.
options: Many of the repairs carried out before 2000 turned out to be unnecessary.
Preventive work tends to be given more credit than it really deserves.
Programmers had exaggerated the danger in order to secure more work for themselves.
The quiet new year may reflect the success of the work, not its pointlessness.
questions.explain: Those who did the work argue that a prevention that succeeds leaves nothing to see, so the uneventful new year, which others took as proof of needless alarm, may in fact show that the repairs did their job. That the repairs were unnecessary is the very conclusion the final sentence answers. The sentence points to the opposite of too much credit: successful prevention risks getting no credit at all, because its success is invisible. Nothing in the text suggests that programmers exaggerated the danger for their own benefit.

questions.prompt: According to the text, why does the low cost of dimming the sun raise a new kind of problem?
questions.passage:
Of all the proposals for dealing with a warming climate, few provoke as much unease as the idea of dimming the sun. The principle is simple enough. Large volcanic eruptions throw fine particles high into the atmosphere, where they reflect a little sunlight back into space, and for a year or two afterwards the world is measurably cooler. A deliberate programme might do the same by releasing particles from high-flying aircraft, and do it, by most estimates, at a cost that is small compared with that of the damage it might prevent.

That cheapness is part of the problem. Cutting emissions requires almost every country to act, and each is tempted to let the others go first. Dimming the sun would require no such cooperation: a single country, or even a wealthy consortium, could in principle attempt it alone. A technology cheap enough for one actor to use raises a question that climate politics has never had to face—not who will pay for action, but who will be allowed to take it, and on whose behalf.

Then there is what such a programme would leave untouched. Reflecting sunlight would offset some of the warming caused by greenhouse gases but would do nothing about the gases themselves. Carbon dioxide would go on accumulating, and the oceans would go on absorbing it and growing more acidic. The cooling, meanwhile, would last only as long as the particles were replenished, since they fall out of the atmosphere within a few years. Were a programme to be stopped abruptly—by war, say, or by a change of government—temperatures could rise towards the level they would have reached without it, and do so far faster than if they had climbed gradually. The world would have bought time on condition of never ceasing to pay for it.

Critics also fear the effect of the idea itself. If governments came to believe that warming could be switched off at will, the argument goes, the pressure to cut emissions would ease. Defenders reply that the same was once said of preparing for floods and droughts: that talk of adaptation would weaken the commitment to prevention. That fear has not obviously come true, and few would now argue that coastal cities should not prepare for higher seas.

For these reasons, even many of those who favour research into the idea present it not as a solution but as something closer to an emergency brake: a measure that one hopes never to use, but that one would rather understand before it is needed than invent in a hurry. Whether studying such a brake makes it more or less likely to be pulled is a question that no experiment can settle. What does seem clear is that a technology this cheap will not remain unexamined simply because the cautious decline to examine it.
options: A single country could try it without the consent of the rest of the world.
Every country would find it far more attractive than cutting its own emissions.
Countries would no longer be willing to share the costs of acting on climate.
It suggests that the risks of the method have been badly underestimated.
questions.explain: Because the method is cheap, 'a single country, or even a wealthy consortium, could in principle attempt it alone', which raises the new question of 'who will be allowed to take' action and on whose behalf. The second paragraph does not claim that every country would prefer the method to cutting emissions; the worry that the idea might weaken the will to cut emissions is raised later, by critics, and concerns the idea itself rather than its cost. Nothing is said about countries refusing to share costs; the point is that cooperation would no longer be needed. Nor does the text link the low cost to underestimated risks.

questions.prompt: According to the text, why can taking on technical debt be a sensible choice?
questions.passage:
Software engineers have borrowed a term from finance to describe a problem that their managers often fail to see. 'Technical debt' is what builds up when a program is written quickly rather than well: a shortcut taken to meet a deadline, a patch added instead of a redesign, a section of code that only its author understands. Like a loan, such a shortcut can be perfectly sensible. A company that ships a rough product in time to win customers may be better off than one that ships a polished product too late. The trouble is that the debt carries interest. Every later change to a tangled program takes a little longer and risks breaking something unexpected, and the cost grows with each new shortcut piled on top of the old ones.

The metaphor has been useful, not least because it gives engineers a language that managers understand. But it can also mislead. A financial debt has a known size and a schedule of payments; technical debt is usually discovered only when someone tries to change the code, and its size may be impossible to estimate in advance. Nor is it always the borrower who pays. Programs often outlive the teams that wrote them, so that the interest falls on people who never took the loan and may not know it exists. Some engineers have therefore suggested that a better comparison would be with pollution: a cost created in one place and quietly passed on to someone else.
options: Tidying up the code later usually costs less than people expect.
Programs built quickly are easier for managers to understand.
Being early can matter more to a business than being thorough.
Shortcuts are usually removed the next time the program is changed.
questions.explain: The text says that 'a company that ships a rough product in time to win customers may be better off than one that ships a polished product too late', so speed can sometimes be worth more than quality. The idea that tidying up later costs less than expected contradicts the claims that the debt 'carries interest' and that its size may be impossible to estimate in advance. What managers understand is the financial metaphor, not programs that were built quickly. And the text describes new shortcuts being piled on top of old ones, not shortcuts being removed when the program is changed.

questions.prompt: What does the author mean by saying that the sceptics 'turned out to be partly right and largely irrelevant'?
questions.passage:
When a team of astronomers first invited members of the public to help sort images of galaxies by shape, many colleagues expected the results to be useless. The volunteers had no training beyond a short online tutorial, and it seemed obvious that their judgements would be less reliable than those of professionals. The sceptics turned out to be partly right and largely irrelevant. Any single volunteer did make more mistakes than an expert. But each image was shown to many volunteers, and the combined verdict of the crowd proved, for most purposes, as good as that of a specialist—and it could be produced for hundreds of thousands of images, a task no team of experts could have completed.

Projects of this kind have since multiplied, from transcribing old ships' weather logs to spotting animals in photographs taken by hidden cameras. Their value does not lie only in the labour they supply. Volunteers, being untrained, sometimes notice what experts have learned to ignore, and several unusual objects have come to light because someone simply asked about something odd in an image. Yet the model has limits. It works best when a task can be broken into many small judgements that are easy to compare with one another, and less well when a judgement requires long experience. It also depends on a supply of enthusiasm that cannot be taken for granted: a project that treats its volunteers merely as unpaid processors tends to lose them.
options: Their doubts were justified at first but faded as the volunteers gained experience.
Volunteers did err more often, but pooling their answers made this matter little.
Their criticism was correct, but few people paid any attention to it at the time.
Volunteers made more mistakes than experts, but only when classifying unusual images.
questions.explain: The sceptics were right that 'any single volunteer did make more mistakes than an expert', but this mattered little, because each image was shown to many volunteers and their combined verdict was, for most purposes, as good as a specialist's. The text says nothing about volunteers gaining experience over time. 'Irrelevant' concerns the importance of the objection, not how much attention it received. And nothing limits the volunteers' mistakes to unusual images; unusual objects are mentioned later as something volunteers sometimes help to find.

questions.prompt: According to the text, how can a sea wall create the need for more walls?
questions.passage:
For centuries the usual answer to a rising sea has been to build a wall. Walls are visible, they protect the land behind them at once, and their benefits are easy to explain to the people whose homes they shelter. They also have a way of creating the need for more of themselves. Land behind a wall feels safe, so it is built on; the more valuable it becomes, the stronger the case for raising the wall again when the sea rises further. Meanwhile, the beach or marsh in front of the wall, unable to move inland as it naturally would, is gradually squeezed out of existence—and with it the natural buffer that once absorbed some of the force of the waves.

An alternative, sometimes called managed retreat, is to allow parts of the coast to flood and to move people and buildings away from the most exposed places in an orderly way. In some places, old sea walls have been deliberately breached so that farmland can turn back into salt marsh, which then helps to protect the land behind it. Engineers often describe such schemes as cheap and effective. Residents tend to describe them differently. To an engineer, a field returned to the sea is a sensible trade; to the family who farmed it, it is a loss that no calculation of averages will make good. The hardest part of retreat is rarely technical. It is deciding who must move, who will pay, and who has the right to decide.
options: It causes the sea along that stretch of coast to rise faster than before.
It weakens as the sea rises and must then be rebuilt in an even stronger form.
It encourages building on land that then becomes too valuable to give up.
It makes residents unwilling to accept any other kind of protection.
questions.explain: Land behind a wall 'feels safe, so it is built on', and the more valuable it becomes, the stronger the case for raising the wall again when the sea rises further. Nothing suggests that a wall makes the sea rise faster; the sea is said to rise in any case. Nor does the text say that walls weaken over time; they are raised because the water gets higher, not because they wear out. And the text does not say that residents refuse other kinds of protection, only that the benefits of walls are easy to explain to them and that residents see managed retreat differently from engineers.

questions.prompt: How does the author interpret Box's remark?
questions.passage:
'All models are wrong,' the statistician George Box once remarked, 'but some are useful.' The line is quoted so often that its second half is easily forgotten. Read in full, the remark is less a complaint that models fall short of reality than a reminder that falling short is what a model is for. A map drawn at the same scale as the country it represents would be perfectly accurate and perfectly useless. What makes a model valuable is precisely what it leaves out: by ignoring most of the world, it lets us see how a few parts of it behave.

This has an awkward consequence. As computers have grown more powerful, it has become possible to build models that leave out very little—simulations of the climate, of an economy or of a living cell that include thousands of interacting processes. Such models can make impressive predictions. But when one of them produces a surprising result, it may be almost as hard to say why as it would be to explain the same event in the real world. A model as complicated as the thing it describes has not been made wrong; it has been made opaque. Many modellers therefore keep simpler versions alongside the elaborate ones, not because the simple ones are more accurate, but because they can be understood, and a result that can be understood can also be questioned.
options: Scientists ought to be more modest about how accurate their models are.
A model remains useful only as long as its errors are kept small.
Most scientific models are too simple to be of any real use.
Leaving out much of reality is what gives a model its value.
questions.explain: The author reads the remark as 'a reminder that falling short is what a model is for' and adds that what makes a model valuable 'is precisely what it leaves out'. A call for modesty about accuracy is the kind of 'complaint' that the author says the remark is not mainly about. Nothing is said about keeping errors small; the map example shows that perfect accuracy can even make a model useless. And the text presents simplicity as a strength, not as a reason why models are of no use.

questions.prompt: What does the author suggest about plans to bring back extinct animals?

questions.prompt: What is the main point of the text?
questions.passage:
Before a state can tax its subjects, conscript their sons or vaccinate their children, it has to be able to find them. This sounds trivial today, when almost everyone has an official name, a registered address and a number that follows them from birth to death. For most of history it was nothing of the kind. In many villages a man might be known by one name to his neighbours, by another in church, and by a description – the miller's son, the one who lives by the bridge – to anyone else. Land was held under customs that the people who used it understood perfectly well and that no outsider could read: a field might belong to one family for ploughing, to the whole village for grazing after the harvest, and to a widow for gleaning the grain that had been left behind.

To an official sent from the capital, such arrangements were less unjust than illegible. They could not be written down in a ledger, compared from one district to the next or added up into a total. Much of what we call the growth of the modern state can be described as a long campaign to make society readable from above. Permanent surnames, which in some countries were imposed by officials rather than chosen by families, made it possible to keep track of individuals across generations. Surveyed maps turned tangled local customs into plots with a single owner and a clear boundary. Standard weights and measures replaced the bushel that varied from one market to the next.

It would be easy to tell this story as one of simple oppression, and some of its episodes deserve no kinder description. But legibility also made possible much that we now take for granted. A pension cannot be paid to someone the state cannot identify, and a vaccination campaign cannot reach children who do not appear in any register. The same records that allowed a government to find young men for its armies later allowed it to find old people who were owed support.

The more troubling lesson lies elsewhere. A simplified picture is useful precisely because it leaves things out, and officials who work with it every day can forget that anything has been left out. When the map is mistaken for the territory, reforms designed on paper can fail in practice – not because their designers were wicked, but because the knowledge that would have warned them existed only in the arrangements they had swept away. The village that shared its fields in complicated ways was often managing risk: no family was ruined by a single bad harvest on one plot. Divided into neat private holdings, the same land could look more rational and leave its owners more exposed.

None of this is an argument against registers or maps. It is an argument for remembering what they are: tools for seeing some things clearly by agreeing not to look at others.
options: Local ways of sharing land were usually fairer and safer than the private plots that officials put in their place.
Making society readable from above has real benefits, but the simplified view it needs can hide what matters.
The rise of the modern state is best understood as a campaign by officials to gain control over unwilling subjects.
Reforms planned on paper tend to fail because officials care more about their records than about the people they govern.
questions.explain: The author describes how states made society 'readable from above', grants that this 'made possible much that we now take for granted', such as pensions and vaccination, and then warns that a simplified picture 'leaves things out', so that reforms can fail because the knowledge that would have warned officials had been swept away. The author explicitly declines to tell the story 'as one of simple oppression', so it is not best understood as a campaign against unwilling subjects. questions.prompt: According to the text, why must musicians' pay rise even though their productivity has hardly changed?
questions.passage:
Why does a haircut cost so much more today than it did fifty years ago, when a television set costs so much less? The usual suspects – greedy hairdressers, rising rents, a lack of competition – explain little. A more convincing answer was offered by the economist William Baumol in the 1960s, and it begins, unexpectedly, with a string quartet.

A string quartet written in the eighteenth century needs four players and takes roughly as long to perform today as it did when it was composed. Over more than two centuries, the productivity of musicians, measured as performances per hour of work, has hardly changed. The productivity of workers who make cloth, cars or telephones, by contrast, has risen many times over. Yet musicians' pay has not stayed where it was. If it had, almost nobody would become a musician; people who might have played the viola would take better-paid work elsewhere instead. Wages in the stagnant sectors must therefore keep roughly in step with wages across the economy, even though productivity there does not. The result is that the cost of a concert, a haircut, a school lesson or a nursing shift rises steadily compared with the cost of goods whose production has become ever more efficient.

Baumol called this a 'disease', but he was careful to point out that it is a strange kind of illness. Services do not become more expensive because anything has gone wrong in them; they become relatively more expensive because something has gone right elsewhere. And because the economy as a whole is growing richer, society can in principle go on affording them. The danger is political rather than economic. When the budgets of schools and hospitals rise faster than inflation year after year, the increase looks like waste, and the natural response is to demand cuts or to search for inefficiencies that may not exist.

Not every service is stuck, of course. Banking and retail have been transformed by computers, and parts of medicine have become far more productive. Some economists also object that measured productivity misses improvements in quality: a hospital stay today may cost more, but it can treat conditions that were once untreatable. Still, the core of Baumol's argument has proved remarkably durable. Wherever the product is essentially human time and attention – teaching a class, caring for an elderly person, performing a play – there is a limit to how much can be saved without changing what is being sold.
options: Concerts have become more popular as people have grown richer.
The music they perform has become more demanding over time.
Otherwise too few people would choose to become musicians.
Concert halls and instruments have become more expensive.
questions.explain: The text says that if musicians' pay had stayed where it was, 'almost nobody would become a musician', because people would 'take better-paid work elsewhere'; wages in such sectors must therefore keep roughly in step with wages in the rest of the economy. Nothing is said about concerts becoming more popular. The text stresses that a quartet takes about as long to perform as it always did, not that the music has become more demanding. And the cost of halls and instruments is never mentioned; rising rents appear only among the 'usual suspects' that the author says explain little.

questions.prompt: According to the text, what did Columbus's critics actually object to?
questions.passage:
Ask people what educated Europeans in the Middle Ages believed about the shape of the earth, and many will say that they thought it was flat, and that Columbus had to overcome fears that his ships would sail off its edge. The story is almost entirely false. Scholars of the period took the earth's roundness for granted; it was taught in the universities and assumed in the most widely used textbooks of astronomy. The objection that Columbus actually faced was quite different and, as it turned out, correct: his critics argued that the earth was much larger than he claimed, so that no ship could carry enough supplies to reach Asia by sailing west. He was saved only because a continent unknown to either side lay in the way.

How, then, did the myth take hold? Historians have traced much of it to the nineteenth century, when popular biographies portrayed Columbus as a lone man of reason facing down superstitious churchmen, and when writers eager to present science and religion as natural enemies found in the flat earth a convenient symbol of the darkness that science had dispelled. The tale suited them too well to be checked.

The irony is that a story told to celebrate critical thinking has survived so long because so few people have thought critically about it. A myth about the credulity of the past turns out to be a fine example of credulity in the present.
options: He could not show that there was any land to the west of Europe at all.
His ships risked being lost at the edge of the known world.
He had greatly underestimated the distance he would have to sail.
His estimate of the earth's size was larger than their own.
questions.explain: The critics 'argued that the earth was much larger than he claimed', so that no ship could carry enough supplies to reach Asia by sailing west; in other words, Columbus had underestimated the distance. The objection was not about whether there was land to the west, since the critics took Asia to lie there; their point was that it was too far away. The fear of being lost at the edge of the world belongs to the false story that the author corrects. And it was the critics, not Columbus, who held the larger estimate of the earth's size.

questions.prompt: How does the author regard Hardin's argument?
questions.passage:
In 1968 the ecologist Garrett Hardin published an essay whose title has outlived most of its arguments: 'The Tragedy of the Commons'. Imagine, he wrote, a pasture open to all. Each herder gains the full benefit of adding one more animal, while the cost – a little less grass for everyone – is shared by all. Every herder therefore has a reason to add animals, and the pasture is grazed to ruin. The essay was widely read as showing that shared resources must either be divided into private property or placed under the control of the state.

The argument is elegant, and under the conditions it assumes – users who never talk to one another and face no rules – it is correct. The trouble is that real commons rarely look like that. The political scientist Elinor Ostrom spent decades studying communities that had managed shared forests, fisheries and irrigation systems for generations without either dividing them up or handing them to a government. What the successful ones typically had in common was not exceptional virtue but structure: clear limits on who could use the resource, rules made by the users themselves, ways of keeping an eye on one another, and penalties that started small and grew with repeated offences.

Ostrom did not claim that self-government always works; she documented failures as well. Her point was that the choice is not limited to two options, and that outsiders who impose one of them can destroy arrangements that were working better than either.
options: As flawed in its logic, since herders would soon see that overgrazing harmed them too
As valid on its own assumptions, which seldom describe how commons are really used
As an accurate account of most commons that overlooks the role of the state
As correct in its own time but made obsolete by modern forms of regulation
questions.explain: The author calls the argument 'elegant' and says that under the conditions it assumes, users who never talk to one another and face no rules, 'it is correct', but adds that 'real commons rarely look like that'. The logic is therefore not said to be flawed. Far from describing most commons accurately, the argument fits few of them, and state control is one of the two solutions the essay was read as recommending, so the state is hardly overlooked. Nor is the argument said to have been made obsolete by modern regulation; the communities Ostrom studied had managed their resources 'for generations'.

questions.prompt: According to the text, what were the original Luddites mainly protesting against?
questions.passage:
The word 'Luddite' is now used for anyone who distrusts new technology, usually with a hint of mockery. The original Luddites, textile workers in parts of England who smashed machines in the 1810s, deserve a fairer hearing. They were not, for the most part, opposed to machinery as such; many had worked with machines all their lives. Their anger was directed at particular employers who used new equipment to replace skilled workers with cheaper, less trained labour, to cut wages and to sell shoddy cloth that undercut the trade. Breaking frames was a way of putting pressure on those employers at a time when workers had no legal right to organise and no vote with which to change the law.

Seen in this light, the Luddites' question was not whether new machines should be used, but who should decide how they were used and who should share in the gains. Economists like to point out that mechanisation eventually made the country far richer and created more jobs than it destroyed, and over the long run they are right. But 'eventually' was a long time. For many of the workers involved, the gains arrived a generation too late, and for their children rather than for them.

That distinction – between what is good for an economy over decades and what happens to particular people in the meantime – is easily lost in today's arguments about automation. Both those who promise that new technology will benefit everyone and those who fear that it will leave millions without work tend to speak as if the outcome were decided by the machines themselves. The Luddites knew better: the outcome was decided by those who owned the machines, and by the laws under which they were used.
options: The use of machinery in a trade that had always been done by hand
Laws that denied them a vote and the right to organise
The way some employers used machines to undermine skilled workers
The poor quality of the machines they were made to operate
questions.explain: The text says that the Luddites were 'not, for the most part, opposed to machinery as such' and that their anger was directed at 'particular employers' who used new equipment to replace skilled workers with cheaper labour and to cut wages. Many of them 'had worked with machines all their lives', so they were not protesting against machinery entering a hand trade. The lack of a vote and of the right to organise explains why they broke frames to put pressure on employers, not what they were protesting against. And the poor quality mentioned in the text concerns the cloth that undercut the trade, not the machines.
