questions.prompt: Why, according to the author, is the explanation that respondents lied 'attractive'?

When an opinion poll gets an election badly wrong, the first explanation offered is usually that people lied: that supporters of an unfashionable party were too embarrassed to admit how they would vote. The explanation is attractive because it flatters the pollsters, implying that their methods were sound and their respondents at fault. Investigations into polling failures, however, have more often pointed to a duller problem: the people who agree to answer a poll are not like the people who do not.

Only a small fraction of those contacted by pollsters today agree to take part. That alone need not matter, as long as the willing are a fair cross-section of the rest. Pollsters adjust their samples so that they contain the right proportions of men and women, young and old, and people from different regions. But if, within each of those groups, the people who answer differ from the people who do not – if they are, say, more interested in politics, or more trusting of institutions – no amount of weighting by age and sex will correct the error. The poll will be precisely balanced and still wrong.

This is why a large sample is no guarantee of accuracy. Asking ten thousand of the wrong people simply produces a smaller margin of error around the wrong answer.
options: It places the blame for the error outside the pollsters' own methods.
It is supported by most investigations into polling failures.
It points to an error that is easier to correct than other kinds of error.
It explains why supporters of small parties are hard to reach.
questions.explain: The author says that the explanation 'flatters the pollsters, implying that their methods were sound and their respondents at fault'. The text says the opposite of the claim that investigations support it: they 'have more often pointed to a duller problem'. Nothing is said about how easy the error would be to correct. And the explanation concerns supporters of an 'unfashionable' party being too embarrassed to say how they would vote, not supporters of small parties being hard to reach.

questions.prompt: What does the author mean by saying that a poll can be 'precisely balanced and still wrong'?

When an opinion poll gets an election badly wrong, the first explanation offered is usually that people lied: that supporters of an unfashionable party were too embarrassed to admit how they would vote. Investigations into polling failures, however, have more often pointed to a duller problem: the people who agree to answer a poll are not like the people who do not.

'Balanced' refers to the make-up of the sample, not to a result that shows two parties level. And the final paragraph says only that a large sample is 'no guarantee of accuracy', not that large and small polls are equally likely to be wrong.

questions.prompt: Why does the author regard the repeated issuing of the English wage laws as significant?
questions.passage: When plague killed perhaps a third or more of Europe's population in the middle of the fourteenth century, it left behind a world with too few hands. Fields went unharvested, and landlords competed for the labourers who remained. In much of western Europe wages rose, and the survivors, especially the poorest, ate better than their grandparents had. Governments responded by trying to turn back the clock. In England, laws were passed that fixed wages at their pre-plague levels and forbade workers to leave their lords in search of better pay. The laws were issued again and again, which is the best evidence that they did not work: there is little point in forbidding what nobody does. Yet the story was not the same everywhere. In parts of eastern Europe, landowners in the following centuries succeeded in tying peasants more tightly to the land than before. The same shortage of labour could strengthen workers or their masters, depending on who held power when it arrived.
options: It shows that landlords supported the laws and wanted them enforced.
It shows that wages had by then fallen back to their earlier level.
It suggests that the laws were made stricter each time they were issued.
It suggests that the laws were widely disregarded.
questions.explain: The author says that the repeated issuing 'is the best evidence that they did not work: there is little point in forbidding what nobody does'. In other words, people kept doing what the laws forbade. The text says nothing about landlords supporting the laws; on the contrary, landlords are said to have competed for the remaining labourers. If wages had fallen back to their earlier level, the laws would have worked, which is the opposite of what the author concludes. And nothing is said about the laws becoming stricter.

questions.prompt: What is the main point of the text?
questions.passage: When plague killed perhaps a third or more of Europe's population in the middle of the fourteenth century, it left behind a world with too few hands. Fields went unharvested, and landlords competed for the labourers who remained. options: The plague made life better for ordinary people throughout Europe.
Governments were unable to control wages in the years after the plague.
How a shortage of workers played out depended on who held power.
Laws that fix wages are bound to fail whenever labour is scarce.
questions.explain: After describing rising wages in western Europe and the failure of the English wage laws, the text turns to eastern Europe, where landowners later tied peasants more tightly to the land, and concludes that 'the same shortage of labour could strengthen workers or their masters, depending on who held power when it arrived'. The improvement for ordinary people is described for 'much of western Europe', not for all of Europe. The English laws failed, but the eastern landowners succeeded, so the text does not present those in power as generally helpless; the failure in England is only part of the argument. For the same reason the text does not claim that wage laws must always fail; it only reports that the English ones did.

questions.prompt: According to the text, why does a life expectancy at birth of thirty-five not mean that most people died at around that age?
questions.passage: It is often said that in earlier centuries people were old at forty and dead by fifty. The figures seem to support this: in many societies before the nineteenth century, life expectancy at birth was somewhere between thirty and forty years. But an average can mislead when the things being averaged are very unequal. In those societies a large share of children died before the age of five, and every death in infancy pulls the average down sharply. A person who survived childhood had a reasonable chance of living into their fifties or sixties, and old people, though far fewer than today, were not curiosities. Much of the rise in life expectancy over the past two centuries reflects not so much longer lives for adults as a far greater chance of reaching adulthood at all.
options: The figure is heavily lowered by the many children who never grew up.
Records from that time tend to understate the age at which people died.
People who reached old age were too few to affect the average.
The figure is based mainly on records of the poorest groups in society.
questions.explain: The text says that a large share of children died before the age of five and that 'every death in infancy pulls the average down sharply', while a person who survived childhood had a reasonable chance of living into their fifties or sixties. Nothing is said about records understating ages or about the figures coming mainly from the poor. And the text does not claim that old people were too few to matter: they were 'far fewer than today' but 'not curiosities', and it is the many early deaths, not the scarcity of old people, that explain the low average.

questions.prompt: Which of the following conclusions is most in line with the text?
questions.passage: It is often said that in earlier centuries people were old at forty and dead by fifty. The figures seem to support this: in many societies before the nineteenth century, life expectancy at birth was somewhere between thirty and forty years. But an average can mislead when the things being averaged are very unequal. In those societies a large share of children died before the age of five, and every death in infancy pulls the average down sharply. A person who survived childhood had a reasonable chance of living into their fifties or sixties, and old people, though far fewer than today, were not curiosities. Much of the rise in life expectancy over the past two centuries reflects not so much longer lives for adults as a far greater chance of reaching adulthood at all.
options: People in earlier centuries aged more slowly than people do today.
Average life expectancy can rise sharply even if adults live little longer.
Old age was about as common in earlier centuries as it is now.
Falling child mortality is the main reason why adults today live longer than before.
questions.explain: The text says that much of the rise in life expectancy 'reflects not so much longer lives for adults as a far greater chance of reaching adulthood at all': since deaths in childhood weigh so heavily in the average, the average can rise a great deal without adults living much longer. Nothing is said about how quickly people aged. Old people are described as 'far fewer than today', so old age was not as common as it is now. And falling child mortality explains the higher average at birth, not longer lives for adults; the text keeps the two apart.

questions.prompt: What 'awkward incentive' does the author point out?
questions.passage: When the number of domestic assaults recorded by the police in a region rises sharply, the headline seems to write itself: violence is on the increase. Yet recorded crime measures two things at once – how often offences occur and how often they reach the police – and the second can change much faster than the first. A campaign that persuades victims to come forward, new training that teaches officers to log incidents they once dismissed as private quarrels, or a change in how offences are counted can all push the figures up while the underlying amount of violence stays the same or even falls. This creates an awkward incentive. A police force that succeeds in winning the trust of victims may look, in the statistics, like a force that is failing to protect them, while one that discourages reports may look like a success. For this reason researchers prefer to compare recorded figures with surveys that ask a sample of the public directly what they have experienced, whether or not they told anyone.
options: Police forces may change how offences are counted in order to keep their figures stable.
Victims may stay silent because they expect officers to dismiss their complaints.
Campaigns that encourage reporting may be blamed for causing more violence.
A police force can come out worse in the figures by doing its job better.
questions.explain: The incentive is explained in the next sentence: a force that wins the trust of victims 'may look, in the statistics, like a force that is failing to protect them', while one that discourages reports may look like a success. Doing the job better can thus make the record look worse. A change in counting is mentioned as one reason why figures can rise, not as something forces do to keep them stable. Officers who dismissed incidents as private quarrels are mentioned in connection with training, but the incentive concerns the police, not the reasons victims stay silent. And the text says that rising figures may be misread as rising violence, not that campaigns are blamed for causing it.

questions.prompt: What does the author conclude about microcredit?
questions.passage: Few ideas in development have risen as fast, or been brought down to earth as firmly, as microcredit. The promise was simple: lend small sums to poor people who have no access to banks, and they will start or expand businesses and lift themselves out of poverty. The loans were repaid at remarkable rates, which seemed to prove that the poor were creditworthy after all. When economists finally tested the idea properly, by comparing similar areas that did and did not gain access to such loans, the results were sobering. Some borrowers did expand their businesses, but on average household incomes rose little, if at all. Yet the same studies found that borrowers valued the loans and used them, among other things, to cope with emergencies and to buy goods they would otherwise have had to save for slowly. Microcredit, it seems, works less as a ladder out of poverty than as a tool for living with it – which is useful, but not what was advertised.
options: It has done the poor little good, since the loans were mostly spent on everyday goods.
It raises the incomes of most borrowers, though by less than its promoters claimed.
It is of real use to the poor, but mainly in a different way from the one promised.
Its high repayment rates show that it lifts many borrowers out of poverty.
questions.explain: The author concludes that microcredit works 'less as a ladder out of poverty than as a tool for living with it', which is 'useful, but not what was advertised': the loans help, for example in coping with emergencies, but not mainly by raising incomes. The text does not say that it has done little good; borrowers 'valued the loans', and buying goods they would otherwise have had to save for is presented as one of the benefits. Nor does it say that most borrowers' incomes rose; on average they rose 'little, if at all'. And the repayment rates only 'seemed to prove' that the poor were creditworthy; the later studies showed that the loans did not, on average, lift borrowers out of poverty.

questions.prompt: According to the text, how can compulsory voting affect the way parties campaign?
questions.passage: Australia is one of a small number of democracies in which voting is compulsory: citizens who fail to vote without a valid reason can be fined, though the fine is small. Turnout at national elections is usually around ninety per cent. Defenders of the system tend to point to the legitimacy that comes from near-universal participation. A less obvious effect concerns how campaigns are fought. Where voting is voluntary, much of a party's effort goes into making sure that its own supporters actually turn up, and a message that excites the faithful, even if it repels everyone else, can be a winning strategy. Where almost everyone votes anyway, there is little to gain from rousing one's own side, and parties must instead win over voters with no strong attachment to either side. Critics reply that compulsion also brings to the polls people who know little and care less, and whose choice may be decided by something as trivial as the order of names on the ballot paper.
options: It gives them reason to focus on voters not firmly committed to any party.
It encourages them to excite their own supporters, since every single vote must be won.
It allows them to spend less on campaigns, since high turnout is already assured.
It leads them to aim their messages at voters who know little about politics.
questions.explain: The text says that where almost everyone votes anyway, 'there is little to gain from rousing one's own side', so parties must 'win over voters with no strong attachment to either side'. Exciting the faithful is described as a strategy that can work where voting is voluntary, which is the opposite case. Nothing is said about parties spending less. And voters who 'know little and care less' appear in the critics' objection about who is brought to the polls, not in the description of how parties campaign.

questions.prompt: What is the main point of the text?
questions.passage: A census looks like the most neutral of government activities: officials simply count who is there. But before anyone can be counted, someone must decide what the categories are, and that decision is rarely neutral. A question about religion, language or ancestry has to offer a list of answers, and the list tells people which identities the state recognises. Groups that appear on the form gain a number, and with it a claim on attention, funding and political representation; groups that do not appear are folded into 'other'. Not surprisingly, the wording of such questions is often fought over long before the census takes place. And once a category has been used for a few decades, it tends to harden: people come to describe themselves in its terms, organisations form around it, and changing it becomes politically difficult even when it no longer fits the way people live.
options: Governments often design censuses so as to reduce the size of unpopular groups.
The way a census sorts people can shape the groups it seems merely to count.
Census categories should be revised often so that they keep up with society.
Groups that are left off a census form tend to disappear within a few decades.
questions.explain: The author argues that deciding the categories 'is rarely neutral': appearing on the form brings a claim on funding and representation, and a category used for decades 'tends to harden' as people describe themselves in its terms and organisations form around it. The census thus helps to shape the groups it appears simply to count. The text does not accuse governments of deliberately shrinking unpopular groups; it says only that groups not listed are folded into the category 'other'. It does not recommend frequent revision either, but notes that change becomes 'politically difficult'. And nothing is said about unlisted groups disappearing; the hardening over decades concerns categories that are used.

questions.prompt: According to the political explanation in the text, why can oil wealth lead to worse government?
questions.passage: Countries that discover large deposits of oil or minerals might be expected to prosper, yet many have grown more slowly, and been governed worse, than neighbours with no such luck. Economists call this the 'resource curse', and several explanations have been offered. One looks at the economy: a flood of export earnings can push up the value of the currency and make farming and manufacturing uncompetitive. Another looks at politics, and turns a familiar slogan on its head. A government that lives on taxes has to keep taxpayers at least partly content, and taxpayers who are asked for money tend to ask, in return, how it is spent. A government that lives on oil revenue needs its citizens far less. It can buy support, pay for a loyal army and ignore demands for accounts, because the money does not come from the people making the demands. The curse, on this view, lies not in the oil itself but in the independence from citizens that it buys.
options: Export earnings strengthen the currency so much that other industries decline.
Oil revenue allows rulers to raise taxes without fear of protest from citizens.
Governments spend their oil money on the army instead of on farming and industry.
Rulers who are not financed by taxes have less reason to answer to citizens.
questions.explain: The political explanation is that a government living on taxes must keep taxpayers 'at least partly content' and answer their questions about spending, whereas one living on oil revenue 'needs its citizens far less' and can 'ignore demands for accounts'. The stronger currency belongs to the economic explanation, not the political one. The text does not say that oil allows rulers to raise taxes; the point is that they do not need taxes at all. And paying for a loyal army is mentioned as one way of staying in power, not as spending taken away from farming and industry, whose decline is part of the economic explanation.

questions.prompt: What does the author mean by the final sentence of the text?
questions.passage: A bank does not keep its depositors' money in a vault. It lends most of it out, keeping only a fraction on hand, on the reasonable assumption that depositors will not all want their money back at once. The arrangement is stable as long as everyone believes that it is. If depositors start to fear that the bank might fail, each of them has a good reason to withdraw before the others do, and the rush to withdraw can bring down even a bank whose loans are perfectly sound. The fear, in other words, can make itself come true. This is why government guarantees of deposits are so effective. If savers know that their money is safe whatever happens to the bank, they have no reason to join a run, and so runs do not start. A guarantee of this kind does its most important work on the days when nobody needs to claim it.
options: Such a guarantee costs governments little, since sound banks rarely fail.
Such a guarantee protects savers mainly on the days when a bank has failed.
Such a guarantee matters most by removing the fear that would start a run.
Such a guarantee works only as long as savers are unaware that it exists.
questions.explain: The text explains that a guarantee is effective because savers who know their money is safe 'have no reason to join a run, and so runs do not start'; its most important work is preventing the fear that would otherwise make depositors withdraw. The text says nothing about what the guarantee costs, and it stresses that even a sound bank can be brought down by a run. The guarantee's main value lies on ordinary days, not on the days when a bank has failed. And it works precisely because savers know about it, since the text says 'if savers know that their money is safe'.

questions.prompt: What is the main point of the text?
questions.passage: Before 1914 it was possible to travel through much of Europe without a passport. Documents existed, and some states demanded them, but for many travellers a ticket and some money were enough to cross several borders. The First World War changed this. Governments worried about spies and deserters, and about who was leaving and entering their territory, introduced strict controls, and when the fighting ended the controls stayed. Within a few years, international conferences were agreeing on a standard format for the passport, including a photograph of its holder, and a document that had been an exceptional measure became an ordinary part of travel. Few people today would describe the passport as a wartime emergency measure, which is perhaps the clearest sign of how completely it has been absorbed into normal life.
options: Passport controls were introduced mainly in order to stop spies and deserters.
A measure introduced in a crisis can outlast it and come to seem normal.
Travel in Europe was freer before 1914 than it has ever been since then.
International cooperation made travel simpler again once the war was over.
questions.explain: The text describes how wartime controls 'stayed' after the fighting ended and how a document that had been 'an exceptional measure became an ordinary part of travel', so that today few people see the passport as an emergency measure at all. Spies and deserters are only part of the governments' worries, which also included 'who was leaving and entering their territory', and the text's point concerns what happened to the controls afterwards, not why they were introduced. The text compares travel only before and after 1914 and makes no claim about every later period. And the international conferences standardised the passport rather than making travel simpler; they helped turn the controls into a permanent feature.

questions.prompt: Why does the author say that the diagnosis 'may be too kind to the decision-makers, or not kind enough'?
questions.passage: When a government keeps pouring money into a project that is plainly failing – a railway that will never carry enough passengers, a computer system that never quite works – commentators reach for the 'sunk cost fallacy': the error of throwing good money after bad because so much has already been spent. The diagnosis may be too kind to the decision-makers, or not kind enough. For the minister who launched the project, abandoning it means admitting a mistake in public, and the admission will be quoted at every election that follows. Continuing, by contrast, postpones the reckoning, perhaps until someone else holds the office. Seen from the minister's chair, carrying on may not be an error of reasoning at all. It may be a perfectly sensible choice – for the minister. The cost of that good sense is borne by the taxpayer.
options: It blames ministers for failures that were usually caused by their predecessors.
It ignores the fact that some projects that seem to be failing succeed in the end.
It assumes that ministers know less about their projects than commentators do.
It calls irrational a choice that may suit the minister but cost the public.
questions.explain: The author argues that carrying on 'may not be an error of reasoning at all' but 'a perfectly sensible choice – for the minister', whose costs are 'borne by the taxpayer'. Calling it a fallacy is thus not kind enough, since it treats ministers as reasoning badly, and too kind, since it presents self-interest as an innocent mistake. The text does not blame failures on predecessors; it is the minister who launched the project who would have to admit the mistake, and only the reckoning may pass to someone else. Nothing is said about seemingly failing projects succeeding in the end; the projects in the text are 'plainly failing'. And the text does not compare what ministers and commentators know.

questions.prompt: Which of the following is most in line with the text?
questions.passage: When doctors, engineers and nurses leave poor countries for better-paid work abroad, the loss seems obvious: the country has paid to educate people whose skills now benefit someone else. Some economists argue that the accounting is less simple. The chance of working abroad, even if only some people will ever take it, can encourage many more to train in the first place, and most of those who train end up staying at home. Those who do leave often send part of their earnings back to their families, and some return years later with savings, experience and contacts. None of this means that emigration is always a gain. Where the departures are concentrated in a few professions, such as medicine in a small country, the remaining shortage can be severe whatever happens to the overall numbers.
options: The prospect of emigrating may leave a country with more skilled people.
Emigration benefits a poor country as long as the emigrants send money back home.
Small countries suffer less from emigration, since fewer of their people leave.
The cost of educating emigrants is usually repaid when they return with savings.
questions.explain: The text says that the chance of working abroad 'can encourage many more to train in the first place' and that 'most of those who train end up staying at home', so the prospect of emigration may increase the number of skilled people in the country. The text says explicitly that emigration is not 'always a gain', and money sent home is only one of several effects, so it does not make emigration a benefit on its own. Small countries are mentioned as places where a shortage in one profession 'can be severe', not as places that suffer less. And only 'some' emigrants return; the text does not say that the cost of their education is usually repaid.

questions.prompt: According to the text, why may signature counts give a misleading picture of literacy in the past?
questions.passage: Historians who want to know how many people could read in, say, the seventeenth century face an obvious problem: reading leaves no trace. What does leave a trace is writing, and in particular the signature. Marriage registers and legal documents show who signed their name and who made a mark instead, and counts of signatures have long served as the standard measure of literacy in the past. The method has the great virtue of being consistent across places and centuries. Its weakness lies in the way children were taught. Reading was usually taught first, and writing, if at all, a year or two later, by which time many children from poorer families had left school to work. A person who made a mark in the register might therefore have been able to read quite well. Signature counts may thus measure one skill accurately while understating another that was more widely shared.
options: Some people who were able to write chose to make a mark instead of signing.
Registers were kept more carefully in some places than they were in others.
Many people who never learnt to write may still have been able to read.
People could learn to sign their names without being able to read at all.
questions.explain: The text explains that reading was usually taught first and writing 'a year or two later', by which time many poorer children had left school, so that a person who made a mark 'might therefore have been able to read quite well'. Nothing is said about people who could write choosing not to sign. The text praises the method for 'being consistent across places and centuries', so it does not point to differences in how registers were kept. And the error the text describes runs the other way: signature counts understate reading ability, rather than counting people who could sign but not read.

questions.prompt: Which of the following would be the most suitable title for the text?
questions.passage:
Ask people where they were when they heard some piece of shocking public news, and many will answer at once and in detail: the room, the person who told them, what they were holding at the time. Psychologists call such recollections 'flashbulb memories', a name that captures how they feel from the inside. They seem to have been recorded in an instant and preserved ever since, complete and unfaded, like a photograph taken by the glare of a flash.

The name, it turns out, flatters them. In a well-known kind of study, researchers ask people to write down how they learned of a dramatic event within a day or two of it happening, and then ask the same people again a few years later. The two accounts often differ, and not only in minor details. Someone who first wrote that she heard the news from a friend in a corridor may later describe, with complete conviction, watching it on television at home. When some participants were shown their own earlier accounts, they did not suddenly remember; a few insisted that the later version must be the right one, although the handwriting was plainly their own.

What sets these memories apart, then, is not their accuracy. Studies that have compared them with memories of ordinary events from the same days have found that both fade and change at a broadly similar rate. The difference lies elsewhere: people remain far more confident about the dramatic memory, and they recall it more vividly. The flashbulb, in other words, lights up our certainty more than it lights up the past.

Why should this be? One likely reason is that such memories are rehearsed. A shocking event is discussed for weeks, replayed in the media and retold at dinner tables, and each retelling is an opportunity for the story to be smoothed, borrowed from or quietly improved. By the time a memory has been told a hundred times, what we recall may be less the original experience than our most recent version of it. Another reason is that we need a place in the story. A public catastrophe is shared by millions; the memory of where we stood when we heard of it is what makes it ours.

None of this means that the memories are worthless, or that the people who hold them are deceiving anyone. They are telling the truth as it now exists for them. But it does suggest a caution that reaches well beyond psychology laboratories. Courts, historians and families all tend to treat a vivid, confident and detailed memory as more trustworthy than a hesitant one. The evidence of flashbulb memories suggests that vividness and confidence are at best weak signs of accuracy—and that the memories we would least think of doubting may be among those most in need of checking.
options: The day the news arrived: how shock sharpens memory
Retelling as a cure for forgetting
Why witnesses to public disasters cannot be trusted
questions.explain: The text argues that memories of shocking public news feel exceptionally clear and certain, but that they change over time as much as ordinary memories do, so that vividness and confidence are 'at best weak signs of accuracy'; a title stressing that such memories are vivid and confident yet often wrong captures this. The idea that shock sharpens memory is the impression the author sets out to correct. Retelling is presented as a likely reason why the memories change, not as a cure for forgetting. And the author does not say that witnesses cannot be trusted; the people who hold such memories are 'telling the truth as it now exists for them', and the advice is only that vivid memories may need checking.

questions.prompt: According to the text, how do flashbulb memories differ from memories of ordinary events?
questions.passage:
Ask people where they were when they heard some piece of shocking public news, and many will answer at once and in detail: the room, the person who told them, what they were holding at the time. Psychologists call such recollections 'flashbulb memories', a name that captures how they feel from the inside. They seem to have been recorded in an instant and preserved ever since, complete and unfaded, like a photograph taken by the glare of a flash.

The name, it turns out, flatters them. In a well-known kind of study, researchers ask people to write down how they learned of a dramatic event within a day or two of it happening, and then ask the same people again a few years later. The two accounts often differ, and not only in minor details. Someone who first wrote that she heard the news from a friend in a corridor may later describe, with complete conviction, watching it on television at home. When some participants were shown their own earlier accounts, they did not suddenly remember; a few insisted that the later version must be the right one, although the handwriting was plainly their own.

What sets these memories apart, then, is not their accuracy. Studies that have compared them with memories of ordinary events from the same days have found that both fade and change at a broadly similar rate. The difference lies elsewhere: people remain far more confident about the dramatic memory, and they recall it more vividly. The flashbulb, in other words, lights up our certainty more than it lights up the past.

Why should this be? One likely reason is that such memories are rehearsed. A shocking event is discussed for weeks, replayed in the media and retold at dinner tables, and each retelling is an opportunity for the story to be smoothed, borrowed from or quietly improved. By the time a memory has been told a hundred times, what we recall may be less the original experience than our most recent version of it. Another reason is that we need a place in the story. A public catastrophe is shared by millions; the memory of where we stood when we heard of it is what makes it ours.

None of this means that the memories are worthless, or that the people who hold them are deceiving anyone. They are telling the truth as it now exists for them. But it does suggest a caution that reaches well beyond psychology laboratories. Courts, historians and families all tend to treat a vivid, confident and detailed memory as more trustworthy than a hesitant one. The evidence of flashbulb memories suggests that vividness and confidence are at best weak signs of accuracy—and that the memories we would least think of doubting may be among those most in need of checking.
options: They change less over the years, although people recall them less vividly.
They are more accurate at first, but they fade faster in the years that follow.
They are no more stable, but people feel surer of them and they seem more vivid.
They are more vivid, and for that reason people tend to retell them more often to others.
questions.explain: Studies comparing the two kinds of memory found that both 'fade and change at a broadly similar rate'; the difference is that people remain far more confident about the dramatic memory and recall it more vividly. The claim that they change less but are less vivid gets both parts wrong: they change at much the same rate and are recalled more vividly, not less. Nothing in the text says that they are more accurate at first and then fade faster; the comparison found a similar rate of change. And although the text says that such memories are retold, it explains this by the event being widely discussed, not by the memory being vivid.

questions.prompt: What is the reviewer's main objection to the exhibition?
questions.passage:
There is a familiar story about late style, and the curators of this exhibition clearly know it by heart. An artist grows old, loses patience with polish and convention, and in the final years produces work that is rougher, freer and more personal than anything before—work that the public of the day mistook for decline and that later generations recognised as the summit. The story has been told of composers, poets and painters alike, and it is now being told, on the walls of four large rooms, about Hendrika Maes, who painted the same stretch of coastline for more than fifty years and died, almost unknown outside her own country, in her late eighties.

The first room is the best argument for going. It hangs a dozen of Maes's early harbour scenes, careful, competent and slightly airless, alongside the sketchbooks she filled at the same time. The sketches are anything but airless. Boats are set down in three strokes, a squall in a smudge of the thumb. Seen together, the two suggest an artist who could already do in private what she would not yet risk in public.

That room, however, sits awkwardly with the argument the rest of the exhibition makes. The final two rooms, devoted to the paintings of her last decade, are presented as a breakthrough: wall texts speak of 'liberation' and of a painter 'finally free to see'. The canvases are certainly bold—sea and sky reduced to a few bands of colour, the horizon sometimes tilted, sometimes gone altogether—and several are very beautiful. But anyone who has just left the sketchbooks will recognise the freedom. It was there fifty years earlier. What changed in old age was not what Maes could see, but what she was willing to show.

That may seem a quibble, yet it matters. The story of late style flatters us, because it lets us believe that age and approaching death bring a kind of wisdom that can be read off the brushwork. It also lets curators skip over the decades in the middle, which here are represented by a single, crowded room. Those were the years in which Maes painted portraits for money, taught in a provincial school and exhibited rarely. They are less romantic than either the careful beginning or the blazing end, and the exhibition treats them as an interval to be walked through quickly. It is precisely there, I suspect, that the answer to the exhibition's real question lies: not how an old woman found her freedom, but why a young one waited so long to use it.

None of this should keep anyone away. The late canvases deserve to be seen at the scale for which they were made, and the sketchbooks alone are worth the ticket. Just be prepared to look past the wall texts. The exhibition has more to tell than the story it has chosen to tell.
options: It treats her late boldness as newly won, though the first room shows she had it decades earlier.
It gives too much space to careful early paintings that do not show Maes at her best and most original.
It hangs the late canvases in rooms that are too small for the large scale at which they were painted.
It overpraises the late paintings, which are in fact less accomplished than the work of her youth.
questions.explain: The reviewer's objection is to the story the exhibition tells: the late rooms present Maes's bold style as a 'breakthrough' and a 'liberation', yet the sketchbooks in the first room show that the same freedom 'was there fifty years earlier'. The reviewer calls the first room 'the best argument for going', so there is no complaint that the early work takes up too much space. The remark about scale is a reason to visit, not a complaint: the late canvases 'deserve to be seen at the scale for which they were made'. And the reviewer finds several late paintings 'very beautiful', without ranking them below the early work.

questions.prompt: What is the writer's main objection to the columnist's argument?
questions.passage:
Sir,

Your columnist's lament for the word 'decimate' (Weekend, 14 March) was entertaining, but I fear it rests on a mistake that is older than the word itself. He objects that people now use 'decimate' to mean 'destroy almost entirely', when it 'really' means to kill one in every ten, as the Roman army is said to have done to punish mutinous legions. By his reasoning, a word means whatever it meant when it entered the language, and every later development is a kind of corruption.

I teach Latin, so I have some sympathy with anyone who enjoys knowing where words come from. But the history of a word is evidence of where it has been, not a ruling on where it may go. 'Nice' once meant foolish; nobody now thinks that a nice afternoon was a stupid one. If your columnist applied his principle consistently, he would have to object to half the words in his own article, starting, I suspect, with several that he has never stopped to look up.

Nor is it obvious that the old sense is the more useful one. The Roman practice, whatever its frequency, ended long ago, and a word that could only describe it would have very little to do. The modern sense, by contrast, fills a real gap: we have many words for destroying things completely, and rather fewer for damaging them so badly that what remains is barely recognisable.

None of this means that anything goes. Words can be misused, and a writer who uses 'decimate' to mean 'slightly reduce' deserves the red pen. But the test is whether the meaning is shared and clear, not whether it would have satisfied a centurion.

Yours faithfully,
Ruth Okafor, Leeds
options: It treats a word's first sense as the standard for judging all later uses.
It relies on a mistaken account of what the Roman army actually did to its soldiers.
It overlooks the fact that 'decimate' is now often used to mean 'slightly reduce'.
It treats Latin as a more important source of English words than any other language.
questions.explain: The writer's complaint is that the columnist treats the meaning a word had when it entered the language as its true meaning and every later development as 'a kind of corruption'; she replies that 'the history of a word is evidence of where it has been, not a ruling on where it may go'. She does not dispute what the Roman army did, and even leaves its frequency open ('whatever its frequency'). Using 'decimate' to mean 'slightly reduce' is something she herself condemns, not a fact the columnist overlooked. And nothing in the letter suggests that the columnist rates Latin above other sources of English; it is the writer who teaches Latin.

Sir,

Your columnist's lament for the word 'decimate' (Weekend, 14 March) was entertaining, but I fear it rests on a mistake that is older than the word itself. He objects that people now use 'decimate' to mean 'destroy almost entirely', when it 'really' means to kill one in every ten, as the Roman army is said to have done to punish mutinous legions. By his reasoning, a word means whatever it meant when it entered the language, and every later development is a kind of corruption.

I teach Latin, so I have some sympathy with anyone who enjoys knowing where words come from. But the history of a word is evidence of where it has been, not a ruling on where it may go. 'Nice' once meant foolish; nobody now thinks that a nice afternoon was a stupid one. If your columnist applied his principle consistently, he would have to object to half the words in his own article, starting, I suspect, with several that he has never stopped to look up.

Nor is it obvious that the old sense is the more useful one. The Roman practice, whatever its frequency, ended long ago, and a word that could only describe it would have very little to do. The modern sense, by contrast, fills a real gap: we have many words for destroying things completely, and rather fewer for damaging them so badly that what remains is barely recognisable.

None of this means that anything goes. Words can be misused, and a writer who uses 'decimate' to mean 'slightly reduce' deserves the red pen. But the test is whether the meaning is shared and clear, not whether it would have satisfied a centurion.

Yours faithfully,
Ruth Okafor, Leeds
options: When it is used about anything other than the killing of people
When it is used in a sense that the word did not have in Latin
When it is given a meaning that readers cannot be expected to share
When a more exact word for complete destruction would serve as well
questions.explain: The writer's test is 'whether the meaning is shared and clear', and her example of misuse is 'decimate' meaning 'slightly reduce', a sense readers would not recognise. She nowhere limits the word to killing people; the modern sense she defends concerns damaging things badly. Judging a use by its Latin sense is the columnist's approach, which she rejects. And her remark about words for complete destruction is an argument that the modern sense fills a gap, not a rule for when the word should be avoided.

questions.prompt: What is the author's view of the complaint about 'literally'?
questions.passage:
Few words provoke as much irritation among careful speakers as 'literally' used to mean its opposite. 'I literally died laughing,' says someone who plainly did not, and a certain kind of listener winces. The objection seems unanswerable: a word whose job is to mark that something is not a figure of speech is being used to decorate a figure of speech, and if it can mean both 'actually' and 'not actually', it would seem to mean nothing at all.

Yet the complaint has a weaker history than its confidence suggests. The intensifying use is not a recent invention of careless teenagers; it can be found in the work of respected novelists more than a century old. More importantly, it follows a path that many other words have taken before it. 'Very' comes from an old French word meaning 'true', and once meant something close to 'truly'; 'really' and 'truly' themselves are now used mostly to add emphasis, not to vouch for accuracy. Speakers seem to have a steady appetite for words that insist on their own sincerity, and the more such a word is used for emphasis, the less it insists. Each wears out and is replaced, and the replacement wears out in turn.

Nor, in practice, does the double meaning cause much confusion. Listeners rarely mistake 'I literally died laughing' for a report of a death, any more than they take 'I'm starving' as a medical claim. Context does the work, as it does for the many words that carry two meanings. What the intensifier does destroy is the usefulness of 'literally' as a precise tool in the rare cases where one needs it: the speaker who wants to say that the floor literally collapsed, not that the evening went badly, may now have to add 'and I mean that literally'. That is a real cost, but it is a cost paid by a few careful writers, not a collapse of meaning, and it is one that the language has paid many times before.
options: It turns a minor loss of precision into a supposed collapse of meaning.
It is fully justified, because the word can no longer mean anything at all.
It is mistaken, because the new use of the word costs the language nothing.
It is fair in substance, but it wrongly blames young people for the change.
questions.explain: The author grants that the intensifying use has 'a real cost', since 'literally' becomes less useful in the rare cases where its strict sense is needed, but insists that this is 'not a collapse of meaning'; the complaint thus inflates a small loss. The view that the word now means nothing is the complaint itself, which the author argues against by showing that context prevents confusion. Saying that the change costs nothing goes too far, since the author admits a real cost. And the author does not accept the complaint in substance; the remark about teenagers is only one of several points made against it.

questions.prompt: According to the text, why do passengers usually stay silent?
questions.passage:
On a crowded morning train, the rule seems to be silence. Passengers sit inches apart, eyes on their phones or the window, and hardly anyone speaks. Most of us explain our own reserve in terms of other people: they would rather be left alone, we assume, and we would not want to impose.

Researchers who have tested that assumption have found it largely mistaken. In experiments of this kind, commuters were asked either to talk to a stranger, to keep to themselves, or to travel as they normally would. Before the journey, most predicted that a conversation would be the least pleasant option. Afterwards, those who had talked reported the most pleasant journeys, and very few had been rebuffed. The strangers, it seemed, were just as willing to talk; they were simply waiting, like everyone else, for someone else to begin.

What keeps the silence in place, then, is not a shared preference but a shared misjudgement. Each passenger underestimates how interested the others would be, and because nobody tests the belief, nobody discovers that it is wrong. Silence confirms itself: the quiet carriage looks like proof that people want quiet.

It would be easy to turn this into a campaign, and some have tried, with badges inviting conversation and posters urging people to say hello. The findings support a more modest conclusion. Some people on some journeys do want to be left alone, and a well-meaning stranger can be a burden. The point is not that we should all talk more, but that we are poor judges of when talking would be welcome, and that our errors tend to run in one direction.
options: Most of them would genuinely prefer to spend the journey alone with their thoughts.
They have learned from experience that strangers seldom welcome being spoken to.
Each of them wrongly expects that the others would not want to be spoken to.
They underestimate how pleasant a journey in silence can turn out to be.
questions.explain: The text describes 'a shared misjudgement': each passenger underestimates how interested the others would be in talking, and since no one tests the belief, no one discovers that it is wrong. The text rejects the idea that the silence reflects a genuine preference ('not a shared preference'). Experience does not teach people that strangers are unwilling, since very few of those who talked were rebuffed; the belief survives precisely because it is not tested. And it is a conversation, not a silent journey, whose pleasantness people underestimate.

questions.prompt: According to the critics described in the text, why could the performances not be truly 'authentic'?
questions.passage:
For most of the twentieth century, a performance of Bach or Handel sounded much like a performance of Brahms: large orchestras, modern instruments, slow tempos and a generous sheen of vibrato. Then a movement of scholars and musicians set out to rescue the older music from these habits. They studied treatises, rebuilt instruments of the period and tried to play the music as its first audiences would have heard it. The results, smaller, lighter and often faster, struck many listeners as a cleaning of an old painting: colours that had been dulled for generations suddenly came through.

The movement's early banner was 'authenticity', and it was this word that drew the sharpest criticism. Critics pointed out that we cannot hear with eighteenth-century ears. A first audience heard a harpsichord against a background of silence that no modern listener, raised on amplified sound, can recover; the same notes, played on the same instrument, cannot mean the same thing to us. Some went further, arguing that the new style owed as much to modern taste as to historical evidence—that its brisk tempos and clean textures sounded suspiciously like the tastes of the late twentieth century, projected onto the past.

The musicians largely accepted the point and quietly dropped the word. What they kept was the practice, and the practice has outlived the quarrel. Few today would claim to be recreating a historical performance, but many conductors of modern orchestras now play Bach with lighter textures and livelier tempos than their predecessors did. The movement failed to prove what it claimed, and succeeded in changing how everyone plays.
options: The instruments of the period could no longer be rebuilt exactly as they had been.
Modern listeners hear the music against a different background of sound.
The musicians relied too much on old treatises and too little on their own taste.
The music's first audiences had heard it played by far larger orchestras.
questions.explain: The critics argued that 'we cannot hear with eighteenth-century ears': modern listeners, used to amplified sound, cannot recover the silence against which the first audiences heard the music, so the same notes cannot mean the same to them. The text does not say that the instruments could not be rebuilt; it says that the musicians rebuilt them. The second criticism runs the other way: the new style was said to owe too much to modern taste, not too little. And the large orchestras belonged to twentieth-century performances, not to the music's first audiences.

questions.prompt: According to the text, what seems to determine whether taking a photograph harms our memory of an object?
questions.passage:
Anyone who has visited a famous painting recently will have seen the scene: a crowd of raised phones, each owner looking at the picture through a screen. It is easy to sneer, and many do. But the habit raises a more interesting question than whether it is rude, namely what it does to the person holding the camera.

Some studies suggest that it does something unexpected. In experiments in museums, visitors who photographed objects later remembered fewer details of them than visitors who had simply looked—as if, knowing that the camera would remember for them, they had felt free to forget. Yet the effect is not simple. When people were asked to photograph a particular detail, zooming in on it, their memory for the object was not impaired in the same way. The difference, it seems, lies less in the camera than in the attention behind it. A photograph taken in order to stop looking costs us something; a photograph taken as a way of looking more closely may cost very little.

If so, the real problem with the crowd at the painting is not the phones themselves. It is that so many of them are being used to tick something off rather than to see it.
options: Whether the person looks at the photographs again after the visit is over
How many photographs the person takes during a single visit
Whether the object photographed is famous or little known
Whether the camera serves as an aid to looking or as a substitute for it
questions.explain: The text reports that visitors who photographed objects remembered fewer details of them, but that those asked to zoom in on a detail did not suffer in the same way, and concludes that the difference 'lies less in the camera than in the attention behind it': a photograph taken 'in order to stop looking' costs us something, while one taken 'as a way of looking more closely' may cost very little. Looking at the photographs afterwards is not mentioned. Nor does the text compare people who take many photographs with those who take few, or famous objects with little-known ones; the famous painting only frames the discussion and plays no part in the studies.

questions.prompt: What does the author suggest about the crowd of phones in front of the famous painting?
questions.passage:
Anyone who has visited a famous painting recently will have seen the scene: a crowd of raised phones, each owner looking at the picture through a screen. It is easy to sneer, and many do. But the habit raises a more interesting question than whether it is rude, namely what it does to the person holding the camera.

Some studies suggest that it does something unexpected. In experiments in museums, visitors who photographed objects later remembered fewer details of them than visitors who had simply looked—as if, knowing that the camera would remember for them, they had felt free to forget. Yet the effect is not simple. When people were asked to photograph a particular detail, zooming in on it, their memory for the object was not impaired in the same way. The difference, it seems, lies less in the camera than in the attention behind it. A photograph taken in order to stop looking costs us something; a photograph taken as a way of looking more closely may cost very little.

If so, the real problem with the crowd at the painting is not the phones themselves. It is that so many of them are being used to tick something off rather than to see it.
options: The main objection to it is that it spoils the view for other visitors.
Many of those taking pictures are recording the painting instead of seeing it.
The pictures taken will probably help the visitors remember the painting later.
Phones should not be allowed in front of the most famous works of art.
questions.explain: The author concludes that the problem is not the phones themselves but that so many are used 'to tick something off rather than to see it', that is, to record having been there instead of looking. The author sets aside the question of rudeness as less interesting, so spoiling the view for others is not the main objection. The studies suggest that photographs taken in order to stop looking weaken memory, so they are unlikely to help. And the author does not call for a ban; the point is about how phones are used.

questions.prompt: According to the text, what did later research show about the 'Mozart effect'?
questions.passage:
In the 1990s a short study reported that students who had listened to a Mozart sonata for ten minutes performed slightly better on a spatial reasoning task than students who had sat in silence. The effect was small and lasted only about a quarter of an hour, but the idea that classical music makes you cleverer proved irresistible. Within a few years, CDs promising to boost babies' intelligence were on sale, and at least one American state governor proposed giving recordings of classical music to new parents.

Later research cut the claim down to size. Attempts to repeat the finding produced mixed results, and where an effect did appear, it was not specific to Mozart. Listeners did about as well after hearing a story they enjoyed, while slow, sad music produced no benefit. What seemed to matter was not the music but the listener's mood and alertness: anything that left people briefly more awake and cheerful helped them a little on the task. The Mozart effect, in other words, was real enough in its original small form, but it was an effect of arousal, not of Mozart.
options: It vanished completely once the experiment was repeated with proper care.
It appeared with classical music of every kind but not with other sounds.
It came from a passing change in mood, not from anything special about Mozart.
It turned out to be stronger in infants than in the university students first studied.
questions.explain: Later studies found that the effect was not specific to Mozart: a story the listeners enjoyed worked about as well, slow, sad music did not, and what mattered was the listener's mood and alertness. The author says that the effect was 'real enough in its original small form', so it did not vanish completely. It was not tied to classical music, since slow, sad music gave no benefit and a story did. And the text says nothing about research on infants; babies are mentioned only as the target of CDs sold after the first study.

questions.prompt: According to the text, how do recent researchers see the link between nostalgia and low mood?
questions.passage:
The word 'nostalgia' was coined in the late seventeenth century by a Swiss medical student to describe an illness. Its sufferers, often soldiers serving far from home, were said to lose their appetite, sleep badly and sometimes waste away from longing for their native valleys. For two centuries doctors treated it as a disease, and even after it lost that status it kept a bad name: a sentimental weakness, a refusal to face the present.

Psychologists who have studied it more recently paint a kinder picture. Nostalgia, they find, tends to arrive when people feel lonely, uncertain or low, and it seems to work less as a symptom of those states than as a response to them. Recalling cherished moments from the past—usually moments shared with others—leaves people feeling more connected to other people and more confident that their lives have meaning. In some studies, it has even made people more optimistic about the future. The yearning for home that once seemed to destroy soldiers may, in milder doses, be one of the ways in which the mind keeps itself steady.
options: Nostalgia is a sign that a person's low mood is growing worse.
Nostalgia tends to make people feel more lonely and cut off from others.
Nostalgia leads people to dwell on the past instead of facing the present.
Nostalgia seems to counter low mood rather than simply reflect it.
questions.explain: The text says that nostalgia tends to arrive when people feel lonely, uncertain or low, but that it works 'less as a symptom of those states than as a response to them': rather than merely reflecting low mood, it counters it, leaving people feeling more connected to others and more confident that their lives have meaning. Nothing suggests that it signals a worsening mood. It makes people feel more connected, not more lonely. And the idea that it is a refusal to face the present is the older view that the recent research is said to correct.

questions.prompt: Why does the author mention a wedding ring?
questions.passage:
When a painting long admired as the work of a great master is shown to be a forgery, something strange happens. The picture on the wall has not changed: every brushstroke is where it was the day before. Yet its price collapses, it is moved to a storeroom, and visitors who once lingered in front of it would now walk past. If we value paintings for what we see in them, this makes no sense.

One explanation is snobbery: we were never really looking, only admiring a famous name. There is surely some truth in this. But it cannot be the whole story, because the reaction is not confined to people who care about prestige. Most of us feel something similar about objects that matter to us personally. A wedding ring replaced by an identical copy is not the same ring, and few people would accept that it was. What we value in such things is partly their history—the fact that this object, and no other, was there. A painting is not only an image but a record of a particular person's hand at work, and a forgery, however skilful, is a record of someone else's.

Seen this way, the collapse in value is not a failure of taste. It is what happens when we learn that we have been told the wrong story about an object.
options: To show that copies of valuable objects are often impossible to tell from originals
To suggest that paintings ought to be valued in the same way as personal belongings
To show that caring about where an object comes from is not merely snobbery
To show that most people care more about prestige than they are willing to admit
questions.explain: The author mentions the ring to support the claim that the reaction to forgeries 'is not confined to people who care about prestige': we value personal objects partly for their history, and a copy, however identical, lacks it. The ring in the example is an identical copy, but the point is not that copies are hard to detect. The author does not recommend how paintings ought to be valued, but uses the ring to explain how they already are. And the example is used against the snobbery explanation, not to show that people secretly care about prestige.

questions.prompt: What does the example of British and American Sign Language show?
questions.passage: It is often assumed that sign languages are a kind of mime, or else a way of spelling out a spoken language with the hands, and that deaf people everywhere must therefore be able to understand one another. Neither assumption holds. Most signs are no more self-explanatory than most spoken words, and a sign language is not a translation of the spoken language around it but a language in its own right, with its own grammar and word order. British and American Sign Language, for instance, are largely unintelligible to each other's users, although the hearing populations of the two countries share a spoken language. Like spoken languages, sign languages have arisen wherever communities have needed them, and they have drifted apart for the same reasons: distance, history and time.
options: Sign languages are harder for hearing people to learn than spoken languages are.
Deaf communities in different countries rarely come into contact with each other.
A shared spoken language is what allows sign languages to be understood across borders.
A sign language is not just the local spoken language put into signs.
questions.explain: The users of British and American Sign Language largely cannot understand each other although the hearing people of the two countries share a spoken language; this shows that a sign language is not the surrounding spoken language turned into signs but 'a language in its own right', with its own grammar and word order. The text says nothing about how hard sign languages are for hearing people to learn, or about how often deaf communities meet. And the example shows the opposite of a shared spoken language making sign languages mutually understandable.

questions.prompt: How does the author respond to the claim that proverbs are worthless?
questions.passage: Proverbs have a reputation for wisdom, but taken together they are remarkably inconsistent. We are told to look before we leap and that he who hesitates is lost; that absence makes the heart grow fonder and that out of sight is out of mind; that many hands make light work and that too many cooks spoil the broth. It would be easy to conclude that proverbs are worthless, since for every piece of advice there seems to be another recommending the opposite. But this is to misunderstand what they are for. A proverb is not a law of nature to be tested against all cases; it is a tool to be picked up when a situation calls for it. Its value lies not in being always true but in being ready to hand, compressing an observation that is true often enough into a form that can be remembered and quoted at the right moment.
options: By pointing out that most proverbs agree with each other once they are properly understood
By arguing that a proverb is meant to be used when it fits, not to hold in every case
By showing that the conflicting proverbs come from different periods and cultures
By admitting that proverbs give poor advice but defending them as memorable sayings
questions.explain: The author argues that a proverb is 'not a law of nature to be tested against all cases' but 'a tool' to be used when a situation calls for it; it need only be true often enough. The author does not deny that proverbs contradict each other, and the opening examples are presented as genuine contradictions. The origins of the proverbs are not discussed. And the author does not concede that proverbs give poor advice; they compress observations that are 'true often enough', and their memorable form is what makes that advice available at the right moment.

questions.prompt: Which of the following findings would best support the view presented in the text?
questions.passage: We tend to think of laughter as a response to humour: someone tells a joke, and we laugh because it is funny. Researchers who have recorded people laughing in ordinary settings—on the street, in cafés, at work—have found that this is the exception. Most laughter follows remarks that are not funny at all, such as 'See you later' or 'I know what you mean', and people laugh far more often in company than alone. It is also usually the speaker, not the listener, who laughs the most. Such findings suggest that laughter is less a reaction to jokes than a social signal, a way of showing friendliness and keeping a conversation going. Humour is one occasion for it, but by no means the most common.
options: People find the same joke less funny when they hear it for the second time.
People laugh more at jokes about familiar situations than at jokes about strange ones.
People watching a comedy alone rarely laugh, even at scenes they find very funny.
People who are good at telling jokes tend to be popular among their colleagues.
questions.explain: The text argues that laughter is less a reaction to jokes than a social signal, pointing out that most laughter follows remarks that are not funny and that people laugh far more in company than alone. A finding that people watching a comedy alone rarely laugh, even at scenes they find very funny, would support this, since the humour is there but, with nobody to signal to, the laughter is not. Findings that a joke is less funny the second time, or that jokes about familiar situations get more laughs, concern what makes jokes funny and so treat laughter as a reaction to humour. And the popularity of good joke tellers says nothing about why or when people laugh.

questions.prompt: According to the reply, why do givers and receivers judge gifts differently?
questions.passage:
Q: My sister has sent me a list of things she would like for her birthday. It feels so impersonal. Wouldn't it be kinder to choose something myself, as a surprise?

A: It may feel kinder, but the evidence suggests that your sister would disagree. When researchers have asked givers and receivers about the same gifts, they have repeatedly found a mismatch. Givers expect an unrequested gift to seem more thoughtful; receivers tend to appreciate the things they actually asked for more, and do not regard them as less personal. The giver is thinking about the moment of unwrapping, when surprise counts for a great deal. The receiver is thinking about the months that follow, when what counts is whether the thing is used. Your sister has told you which of these she cares about. If you want to add a personal touch, a short note will do it better than a guess.
options: Givers think of the moment of opening, receivers of the use the gift gets later.
Givers tend to spend more money on gifts that the receiver has not asked for.
Receivers often feel awkward about being given exactly the things they asked for.
Receivers value being surprised more highly than most givers tend to expect.
questions.explain: The reply explains the mismatch by saying that the giver is thinking about 'the moment of unwrapping', when surprise counts, while the receiver is thinking about the following months, when what counts is whether the gift is used. Nothing is said about how much givers spend. Receivers are said to appreciate requested gifts more and not to regard them as less personal, so they do not feel awkward about them. And it is givers, not receivers, who place great weight on surprise.

questions.prompt: Why does the author mention that people reread favourite books and rewatch favourite films?
questions.passage: Most people go to some lengths to avoid hearing how a film or novel ends, and many regard a friend who gives it away as having robbed them of something. Yet when readers in one series of experiments were given short stories, some with a paragraph revealing the outcome placed at the start, many of those who knew the ending in advance reported enjoying the stories more, not less. One possible explanation is that knowing where a story is going frees the reader to attend to how it gets there: the language, the hints, the small ironies that a first-time reader, hurrying towards the outcome, may miss. That would also explain why people happily reread favourite books and rewatch favourite films whose endings they know perfectly well. Suspense, on this view, is only one of the pleasures of a story, and perhaps not the greatest.
options: As an example of how suspense can return even when the ending is already well known
To suggest that some readers in the experiments had read the stories before
To show that people tend to forget how a story ends after some time has passed
As further evidence that knowing the ending need not spoil enjoyment of a story
questions.explain: The author suggests that knowing the outcome frees readers to enjoy how a story unfolds, and adds that this 'would also explain' why people happily reread and rewatch stories whose endings they know well; the rereading is thus offered as further support for the view that knowing the ending need not spoil a story. The text does not suggest that suspense returns; on the contrary, it presents suspense as only one of a story's pleasures. Nothing indicates that the readers in the experiments knew the stories beforehand. And the text says that people know the endings 'perfectly well', not that they have forgotten them.

questions.prompt: What does the writer mean by saying that leaving out those who listen to books 'does not measure reading; it measures eyesight'?
questions.passage:
Sir,

In your recent survey of reading habits you counted only printed and electronic books, on the grounds that listening to an audiobook 'is not really reading'. As someone who has lost much of her sight, I would like to know what it is instead. When I listen to a novel, I follow the same plot, meet the same characters and, I am told by friends who have read it in print, come away with much the same understanding. Your reporter may have meant that reading with the eyes exercises particular skills, such as decoding written words, and that is true; it matters a great deal for a child learning to read. But that is not the reason most adults pick up a novel. If the question is whether people are still taking in long and demanding stories, then those who listen belong in your figures. Leaving them out does not measure reading; it measures eyesight.

Yours faithfully,
Margaret Ellison, Norwich
options: The survey mainly reached people whose eyesight happened to be good.
The survey ought to have asked people about the state of their eyesight.
The figures show who can read print rather than who takes in books at all.
People with poor eyesight generally read fewer books than other people do.
questions.explain: The writer argues that people who listen follow long and demanding stories just as readers of print do, so a survey that excludes them ends up recording who is able to read with their eyes rather than who is actually taking in books. Nothing in the letter says whom the survey reached, and the writer does not ask for questions about eyesight; the word is used to describe what the figures end up showing. And the writer's point is that people with poor sight do take in books, but by listening, so the claim that they read fewer books is exactly the impression the survey wrongly creates.

questions.prompt: According to the text, why can a full stop at the end of a short message seem unfriendly?
questions.passage: Written messages have always struggled to carry tone. In speech, a sentence such as 'Fine, see you then' can sound warm, weary or furious depending on how it is said; on a screen it is just four words. Letter writers had time and space to make their attitude clear. The short, rapid messages of today have neither, and their writers have improvised. A full stop at the end of a one-line reply, once simply correct, now strikes many younger readers as curt or even hostile, precisely because it is unnecessary: in a medium where the line break already marks the end, the full stop seems to have been added on purpose. Small faces and symbols, often dismissed as childish, do the work that tone of voice does in speech. They are less a decline in writing than an addition to it.
options: Younger readers were never properly taught how punctuation is supposed to be used.
Because nothing calls for it, readers take it to have been added deliberately.
It makes a short and friendly message look like part of a stiff and formal letter.
It is mostly used by writers who are already annoyed with the person they are writing to.
questions.explain: The text says that a full stop at the end of a one-line reply strikes many younger readers as curt 'precisely because it is unnecessary': since the line break already marks the end, the full stop seems to have been added on purpose. The text does not claim that younger readers have not learned the rules; it says the full stop was 'once simply correct'. Letters are mentioned only as a medium in which writers had time and space to make their attitude clear, not as something a full stop calls to mind. And nothing is said about the full stop being used mainly by writers who are annoyed; the point is how readers interpret it.

questions.prompt: Hur mycket skog avverkades i Götaland säsongen 2000/01?
questions.explain: Använd cirkeldiagrammet för 2000/01, där den totala avverkningen är 60,2 miljoner m³sk. Götaland är den vita sektorn, som går från ungefär klockan åtta till klockan tolv. Den är drygt en tredjedel av cirkeln, cirka 35 procent. 0,35 · 60,2 ≈ 21 miljoner m³sk, så det närmaste alternativet är 20 miljoner m³sk. 35 miljoner lockar om man tar andelen i procent som mängden, och 30 miljoner skulle vara halva cirkeln.

questions.prompt: Hur mycket skog slutavverkades och gallrades sammanlagt 1995?
questions.explain: Använd linjediagrammet och läs av vid 1995. Kurvan för slutavverkning ligger på ungefär 37 miljoner m³sk och kurvan för gallring på ungefär 18 miljoner m³sk. Sammanlagt blir det cirka 37 + 18 = 55 miljoner m³sk. 37 miljoner är bara slutavverkningen, och 66 miljoner är den totala avverkningen, som också innehåller övrig avverkning.

questions.prompt: Hur många fler var de som hade gymnasial utbildning som högsta utbildningsnivå än de som hade eftergymnasial utbildning (ej forskarutbildning) som högsta utbildningsnivå?

Eftergymnasial utbildning: 845 694 (kortare än 3 år) + 1 029 113 (minst 3 år) = 1 874 807; forskarutbildningen står i en egen kolumn och räknas inte med. Skillnaden är 2 937 395 − 1 874 807 = 1 062 588. Talet 1 874 808 är ungefär antalet med eftergymnasial utbildning, inte skillnaden.

questions.explain: Bland raderna för män+kvinnor är 35–44 år störst, med 1 274 179 personer i kolumnen Befolkning. Högre än gymnasial utbildning är eftergymnasial utbildning och forskarutbildning: 207 719 + 231 166 + 15 251 = 454 136. Andelen är 454 136/1 274 179 ≈ 0,36, alltså ungefär 35 procent.

questions.prompt: För hur stor andel av paren där kvinnan var 30–34 år gällde att mannen var yngre än kvinnan?
